notes.front: What is an engine’s power-to-weight ratio, which the handbook also calls its specific weight?
notes.back: The engine’s weight for each brake horsepower it delivers.
notes.explanation: Every excess pound of engine weight reduces the aircraft’s performance, so a lighter engine for the same power is better.
notes.example: Like two engines of equal power where one weighs less: the lighter one has the better ratio and leaves more useful load.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Power & Weight”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: If the weight of an engine per brake horsepower (called the specific weight of the engine) is decreased, the useful load that an aircraft can carry and the performance of the aircraft obviously are increased.

notes.front: What is an inline engine?
notes.back: An engine, usually with an even number of cylinders, with one crankshaft above or below the cylinders.
notes.explanation: When it is built to run with the cylinders below the crankshaft, it is called an inverted engine.
notes.example: Like a single straight row of cylinders along the crankshaft, as in the very old light aircraft that used them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Inline Engines”, p. 1-3
notes.evidence: An inline engine generally has an even number of cylinders, although some three-cylinder engines have been constructed. This engine may be either liquid cooled or air cooled and has only one crank shaft, which is located either above or below the cylinders.

notes.front: What is a horizontally opposed (O-type) engine?
notes.back: An engine with two banks of cylinders directly opposite each other and one crankshaft in the centre, usually mounted horizontally.
notes.explanation: The pistons of both banks drive the single crankshaft, and the air-cooled version is the one used predominantly in aviation.
notes.example: Like the flat four- and six-cylinder engines that most small general aviation aircraft use.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Opposed or O-Type Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: The opposed-type engine has two banks of cylinders directly opposite each other with a crankshaft in the center. [Figure 1-1] The pistons of both cylinder banks are connected to the single crankshaft.

notes.front: What is a V-type engine?
notes.back: An engine with its cylinders in two inline banks, generally set 60° apart.
notes.explanation: Most had 12 cylinders; the type was used mostly during the Second World War, so today it is mostly limited to older aircraft.
notes.example: Like two inline engines leaning away from each other so that, seen from the front, their banks form a V.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “V-Type Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: In V-type engines, the cylinders are arranged in two inline banks generally set 60° apart. Most of the engines have 12 cylinders, which are either liquid cooled or air cooled.

notes.front: What is a radial engine?
notes.back: An engine with a row, or rows, of cylinders arranged radially about a central crankcase.
notes.explanation: The design has proven very rugged and dependable, though its use today is limited.
notes.example: Like the spokes of a wheel, with a cylinder on each spoke, as on the round engines of some older cargo aircraft and crop sprayers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Radial Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: The radial engine consists of a row, or rows, of cylinders arranged radially about a central crankcase. [Figure 1-2] This type of engine has proven to be very rugged and dependable.

notes.front: What is the crankcase of a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: The engine’s foundation: it holds the bearings in which the crankshaft turns and forms a tight enclosure for the lubricating oil.
notes.explanation: It also supports the cylinder assemblies and attaches the powerplant to the aircraft, so it must be rigid enough to keep the crankshaft aligned.
notes.example: Like the frame of a house: the cylinders, crankshaft bearings and engine mounts all attach to it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankcase Section”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: The foundation of an engine is the crankcase. It contains the bearings and bearing supports in which the crankshaft revolves. Besides supporting itself, the crankcase must provide a tight enclosure for the lubricating oil

notes.front: What is the accessory section of a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: The rear section, usually cast in aluminium alloy or magnesium, with mounts for accessories such as magnetos, pumps, starter and generator.
notes.explanation: Drive shafts carried out to its mounting pads let gear ratios give each accessory the proper drive speed.
notes.example: Like a tool board at the back of the engine, holding the magnetos, fuel and oil pumps, starter and generator where they are easy to reach.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Accessory Section”, p. 1-7
notes.evidence: The accessory (rear) section usually is of cast construction and the material may be either aluminum alloy, which is used most widely, or magnesium, which has been used to some extent. On some engines, it is cast in one piece and provided with means for mounting the accessories

notes.front: What is the crankshaft of a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: The engine’s backbone: a shaft of one or more cranks that turns the pistons’ reciprocating motion into rotary motion for the propeller.
notes.explanation: It takes most of the forces the engine develops, which is why it is generally forged from a very strong alloy such as chromium-nickel-molybdenum steel.
notes.example: Like the pedal crank of a bicycle, but with a crank for each cylinder or each row of cylinders.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshafts”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: The crankshaft is the backbone of the reciprocating engine. It is subjected to most of the forces developed by the engine. Its main purpose is to transform the reciprocating motion of the piston and connecting rod into rotary motion for rotation of the propeller.

notes.front: What is a dynamic damper on a crankshaft?
notes.back: A pendulum fastened to the crankshaft so that it can swing in a small arc, used to reduce vibration.
notes.explanation: It is built into the flyweight assembly, and some crankshafts carry two or more, each on a different crank cheek.
notes.example: Like a weight hung from a swaying tower that swings out of step with the tower and so calms it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dynamic Dampers”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: To reduce vibration to a minimum during engine operation, dynamic dampers are incorporated on the crankshaft. A dynamic damper is merely a pendulum that is fastened to the crankshaft so that it is free to move in a small arc.

notes.front: What is a connecting rod?
notes.back: The link that transmits forces between the piston and the crankshaft.
notes.explanation: It must stay rigid under load yet be light, to limit the inertia forces as the rod and piston stop and reverse at each end of the stroke.
notes.example: Like a cyclist’s shin, linking the up-and-down knee to the turning pedal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Connecting Rods”, p. 1-9
notes.evidence: The connecting rod is the link that transmits forces between the piston and the crankshaft. [Figure 1-10] Connecting rods must be strong enough to remain rigid under load

notes.front: What is a master-and-articulated rod assembly?
notes.back: In a radial engine, one master rod per row links a piston to the crankshaft; articulated rods link the row’s other pistons to it.
notes.explanation: The articulated rods hang from flanges on the master rod’s big end, which alone carries the crankpin bearing.
notes.example: Like one strong main spoke riding on the hub, with the other spokes hinged to it rather than to the hub.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Master-and-Articulated Rod Assembly”, p. 1-9
notes.evidence: In a radial engine, the piston in one cylinder in each row is connected to the crankshaft by a master rod. All other pistons in the row are connected to the master rod by articulated rods.

notes.front: What is a knuckle pin?
notes.back: The pin that attaches an articulated rod to the master rod’s flange.
notes.explanation: The pins are pressed into holes in the master rod flanges during assembly, and a lock plate on each side stops them moving sideways.
notes.example: Like the hinge pin of a door, but joining each articulated rod to the master rod.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Master-and-Articulated Rod Assembly”, p. 1-10
notes.evidence: The articulated rods are attached to the master rod by knuckle pins, which are pressed into holes in the master rod flanges during assembly.

notes.front: What is a plain-type connecting rod?
notes.back: A rod used in inline and opposed engines whose crankpin end is fitted with a cap and a two-piece bearing.
notes.explanation: The cap is held on by bolts or studs, one rod per crankpin.
notes.example: Like one rod per piston, each clamped round its crankpin by its own bolted cap.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Plain-Type Connecting Rods”, p. 1-11
notes.evidence: Plain-type connecting rods are used in inline and opposed engines. The end of the rod attached to the crankpin is fitted with a cap and a two-piece bearing.

notes.front: What is a fork-and-blade rod assembly?
notes.back: A rod pair used mainly in V-type engines: the forked rod is split at the crankpin end so the blade rod fits between its prongs.
notes.explanation: A single two-piece bearing serves both rods on the crankshaft end; the type is not used much on modern engines.
notes.example: Like a tuning fork with a flat blade slotted between its prongs, both riding on one crankpin.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Fork-and-Blade Rod Assembly”, p. 1-11
notes.evidence: The fork-and-blade rod assembly is used primarily in V-type engines. The forked rod is split at the crankpin end to allow space for the blade rod to fit between the prongs.

notes.front: What is the piston of a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: A cylindrical part that moves back and forth in the cylinder, acting as a moving wall of the combustion chamber.
notes.explanation: Its force is passed to the crankshaft through the connecting rod.
notes.example: Like the plunger of a syringe: moving down it draws the charge in, moving up it squeezes it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pistons”, p. 1-11
notes.evidence: The piston of a reciprocating engine is a cylindrical member which moves back and forth within a steel cylinder. [Figure 1-13] The piston acts as a moving wall within the combustion chamber.

notes.front: What is a piston pin, also called a wristpin?
notes.back: The tubular pin that joins the piston to the connecting rod.
notes.explanation: It is called a wristpin because the relative motion of piston and rod resembles that of the human arm.
notes.example: Like the pin of a hinge, letting the rod swing while the piston slides.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Pin”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The piston pin joins the piston to the connecting rod. It is machined in the form of a tube from a nickel steel alloy forging, casehardened, and ground. The piston pin is sometimes called a wristpin

notes.front: What does a piston ring do?
notes.back: It seals gas pressure in the combustion chamber and limits oil seeping into it, springing out from its groove against the cylinder wall.
notes.explanation: When properly lubricated, the rings form an effective gas seal.
notes.example: Like a split washer sprung open inside a tube, pressing outward all the way round.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Rings”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The piston rings prevent leakage of gas pressure from the combustion chamber and reduce to a minimum the seepage of oil into the combustion chamber. [Figure 1-15] The rings fit into the piston grooves but spring out to press against the cylinder walls

notes.front: What is a compression ring?
notes.back: A piston ring, in the grooves immediately below the piston head, that stops combustion gases escaping past the piston.
notes.explanation: Most aircraft engines use two compression rings plus one or more oil control rings.
notes.example: Like the top seal of a pump plunger, holding back the pressure above it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Ring”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The purpose of the compression rings is to prevent the escape of combustion gases past the piston during engine operation. They are placed in the ring grooves immediately below the piston head.

notes.front: What is an oil control ring?
notes.back: A piston ring that regulates the thickness of the oil film on the cylinder wall.
notes.explanation: Too much oil in the combustion chamber burns and leaves a thick carbon coating on the chamber walls, piston head, spark plugs and valve heads.
notes.example: Like a wiper blade that leaves just a thin film on the glass.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Oil Control Rings”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: Oil control rings regulate the thickness of the oil film on the cylinder wall. If too much oil enters the combustion chamber, it burns and leaves a thick coating of carbon

notes.front: What is an oil scraper ring?
notes.back: A piston ring, usually with a bevelled face, fitted in the groove at the bottom of the piston skirt.
notes.explanation: It is fitted at the base of the skirt to prevent excessive oil consumption.
notes.example: Like a squeegee at the foot of the piston, its scraping edge set up or down as the cylinder position and engine series require.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Oil Scraper Ring”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The oil scraper ring usually has a beveled face and is installed in the groove at the bottom of the piston skirt.

notes.front: What is the cylinder of a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: The part where power is developed: it provides the combustion chamber and houses the piston and connecting rod.
notes.explanation: In an air-cooled engine it is an assembly of two major parts, the cylinder head and the cylinder barrel.
notes.example: Like a lidded can: the aluminium head is the lid and the steel barrel the can.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinders”, p. 1-14
notes.evidence: The portion of the engine in which the power is developed is called the cylinder. [Figure 1-16] The cylinder provides a combustion chamber where the burning and expansion of gases take place, and it houses the piston and the connecting rod.

notes.front: What is the purpose of the cylinder head?
notes.back: To provide a place for combustion of the air-fuel mixture and give the cylinder more heat conductivity for cooling.
notes.explanation: Air-cooled heads are generally aluminium alloy, a good conductor of heat whose light weight reduces engine weight.
notes.example: Like the finned lid of a pot, where the cooking happens and the heat is shed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Heads”, p. 1-14
notes.evidence: The purpose of the cylinder head is to provide a place for combustion of the air-fuel mixture and to give the cylinder more heat conductivity for adequate cooling.

notes.front: What is the cylinder barrel?
notes.back: The steel-alloy forging in which the piston runs, with its inner surface hardened against wear.
notes.explanation: The hardening resists wear from the piston and the piston rings bearing against the wall.
notes.example: Like a gun barrel with cooling fins machined round its outside.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Barrels”, p. 1-15
notes.evidence: The cylinder barrel is made of a steel alloy forging with the inner surface hardened to resist wear of the piston and the piston rings which bear against it.

notes.front: What is an engine’s firing order?
notes.back: The sequence in which the power event occurs in the different cylinders.
notes.explanation: It is designed for balance and to eliminate vibration as far as possible.
notes.example: Like the order in which a drummer strikes the drums, spread so no side gets two beats in a row.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Firing Order”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: The firing order of an engine is the sequence in which the power event occurs in the different cylinders. The firing order is designed to provide for balance and to eliminate vibration to the greatest extent possible.

notes.front: What is a poppet valve?
notes.back: The conventional aircraft engine valve: a head that opens and closes a cylinder port.
notes.explanation: By shape, poppet valves are called mushroom or tulip valves, after the plants they resemble.
notes.example: Like a mushroom-shaped plug lifted out of a hole and pushed back to seal it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valves”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: The head of each valve opens and closes these cylinder ports. The valves used in aircraft engines are the conventional poppet type.

notes.front: What is a sodium-filled valve?
notes.back: A valve whose hollow stem is partly filled with metallic sodium to carry heat away from the valve head.
notes.explanation: Sodium is used because it is an excellent heat conductor.
notes.example: Like a heat pipe built into the valve stem.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Construction”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: Some intake and exhaust valve stems are hollow and partially filled with metallic sodium. This material is used because it is an excellent heat conductor.

notes.front: What is a cam ring?
notes.back: A circular piece of steel with lobes on its outer surface that operates the valves of a radial engine.
notes.explanation: It is mounted concentrically with the crankshaft and driven by it at a reduced speed.
notes.example: Like a camshaft bent into a hoop round the crankshaft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cam Rings”, p. 1-19
notes.evidence: The cam ring is a circular piece of steel with a series of cams or lobes on the outer surface.

notes.front: What is the camshaft of an opposed engine?
notes.back: The lobed shaft that operates the valves, driven by a gear that mates with a gear on the crankshaft.
notes.explanation: As it turns, its lobes lift the tappets, and the push rods and rocker arms pass that lift to the valves.
notes.example: Like the drum of a music box, whose bumps lift each lever in turn.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Camshaft”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: The valve mechanism of an opposed engine is operated by a camshaft. The camshaft is driven by a gear that mates with another gear attached to the crankshaft.

notes.front: What is a solid lifter?
notes.back: A cam follower whose valve clearance must be adjusted manually with a screw and lock nut.
notes.explanation: The clearance lets the valve close completely, so checking it was a continuous maintenance task until hydraulic lifters came in.
notes.example: Like a fixed spacer between cam and push rod, whose gap someone has to set by hand.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Solid Lifters/Tappets”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: Solid lifters or cam followers generally require the valve clearance to be adjusted manually by adjusting a screw and lock nut.

notes.front: What is a hydraulic valve lifter?
notes.back: A tappet that automatically keeps the valve clearance at zero, so no clearance adjustment mechanism is needed.
notes.explanation: Oil trapped in its pressure chamber acts as a cushion while the valve is lifted.
notes.example: Like a self-adjusting spacer that pumps itself up with engine oil to take up any slack.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hydraulic Valve Tappets/Lifters”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: Some aircraft engines incorporate hydraulic tappets that automatically keep the valve clearance at zero, eliminating the necessity for any valve clearance adjustment mechanism.

notes.front: What is a push rod?
notes.back: A tubular rod that transmits the lifting force from the valve tappet to the rocker arm.
notes.explanation: The tube is light and strong and lets pressurised oil pass through to lubricate the ball ends, rocker bearing and valve guide.
notes.example: Like a hollow drinking straw with a steel ball at each end, carrying both force and oil.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Push Rod”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: The push rod, tubular in form, transmits the lifting force from the valve tappet to the rocker arm.

notes.front: What is a rocker arm?
notes.back: A pivoted arm passing lifting force from the cams to the valves; one end bears on the push rod, the other on the valve stem.
notes.explanation: An adjusting screw on some arms sets the clearance to the valve stem tip so that the valve closes fully.
notes.example: Like a seesaw: the push rod lifts one end and the other end presses the valve open.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Rocker Arms”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: The rocker arms transmit the lifting force from the cams to the valves. [Figure 1-31] Rocker arm assemblies are supported by a plain, roller, or ball bearing, or a combination of these, which serves as a pivot. Generally, one end of the arm bears against the push rod and the other bears on the valve stem.

notes.front: What is a plain bearing, and where is it used in a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: A bearing of non-ferrous metal such as silver or bronze, used for the crankshaft, camshaft, connecting rods and accessory drives.
notes.explanation: Such bearings usually take radial loads only, though some are designed to take thrust loads.
notes.example: Like a smooth sleeve a shaft slides round in, with no balls or rollers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Plain Bearings”, p. 1-22
notes.evidence: Plain bearings are generally used for the crankshaft, cam ring, camshaft, connecting rods, and the accessory drive shaft bearings. Such bearings are usually subjected to radial loads only, although some have been designed to take thrust loads. Plain bearings are usually made of nonferrous (having no iron) metals, such as silver, bronze

notes.front: What is a ball bearing assembly made of?
notes.back: Grooved inner and outer races, one or more sets of balls, and a bearing retainer.
notes.explanation: The surfaces roll over each other rather than slide, and this type can accept both radial and thrust loads.
notes.example: Like a ring of marbles trapped between two grooved hoops.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ball Bearings”, p. 1-22
notes.evidence: A ball bearing assembly consists of grooved inner and outer races, one or more sets of balls, in bearings designed for disassembly, and a bearing retainer.

notes.front: What loads do straight and tapered roller bearings take?
notes.back: Straight roller bearings take radial loads only; tapered roller bearings, with cone-shaped races, take radial and thrust loads.
notes.explanation: The cone shape of the tapered bearing’s races is what lets it resist thrust as well.
notes.example: Like a ring of short rolling pins between two races, straight or cone-shaped.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Roller Bearings”, p. 1-22
notes.evidence: Straight roller bearings are used where the bearing is subjected to radial loads only. In tapered roller bearings, the inner- and outer-race bearing surfaces are cone-shaped. Such bearings withstand both radial and thrust loads.

notes.front: What does propeller reduction gearing do?
notes.back: It lets the engine run at higher rpm, developing more power, while slowing the propeller.
notes.explanation: Propeller efficiency decreases rapidly as blade-tip speed approaches the speed of sound, and the gearing prevents that loss.
notes.example: Like a small gear driving a larger one: the engine spins fast while the propeller turns more slowly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Propeller Reduction Gearing”, p. 1-23
notes.evidence: Reduction gearing for engines allows the engine to operate at a higher rpm, developing more power while slowing down the propeller rpm. This prevents the propeller efficiency from decreasing.

notes.front: What is the four-stroke cycle?
notes.back: An operating cycle of four piston strokes (intake, compression, power, exhaust) taking two crankshaft revolutions; also called the Otto cycle.
notes.explanation: The vast majority of certified aircraft reciprocating engines use it, partly because it lends itself readily to high performance through supercharging.
notes.example: Like a four-beat bar of music: in, squeeze, bang, out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Four-Stroke Cycle”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: The vast majority of certified aircraft reciprocating engines operate on the four-stroke cycle, sometimes called the Otto cycle after its originator, a German physicist.

notes.front: What is top dead centre (TDC)?
notes.back: The top end of the piston’s travel; a stroke runs from top dead centre to bottom dead centre or back.
notes.explanation: Valve and ignition timings are given in degrees of crankshaft travel before or after these two points.
notes.example: Like the top of a swing’s arc, where it stops for an instant before coming back.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Operating Principles”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: The stroke is the distance the piston moves from one end of the cylinder to the other, specifically from top dead center (TDC) to bottom dead center (BDC), or vice versa.

notes.front: What happens on the intake stroke?
notes.back: The crankshaft pulls the piston down, lowering cylinder pressure so that air at atmospheric pressure flows in and brings the metered fuel with it.
notes.explanation: The weight of the charge taken in depends on how far the throttle is open.
notes.example: Like drawing back a syringe plunger to fill it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Intake Stroke”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: During the intake stroke, the piston is pulled downward in the cylinder by the rotation of the crankshaft. This reduces the pressure in the cylinder and causes air under atmospheric pressure to flow through the carburetor, which meters the correct amount of fuel.

notes.front: What happens on the compression stroke?
notes.back: With the intake valve closed, the rising piston compresses the air-fuel mixture.
notes.explanation: An electric spark fires the charge as the piston approaches TDC.
notes.example: Like pushing a syringe plunger in with your finger over the tip.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Stroke”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: After the intake valve is closed, the continued upward travel of the piston compresses the air-fuel mixture to obtain the desired burning and expansion characteristics. The charge is fired by means of an electric spark as the piston approaches TDC.

notes.front: What happens on the power stroke?
notes.back: The rapidly expanding burning gases push the piston down from TDC.
notes.explanation: The connecting rod’s downward movement is changed to rotary movement by the crankshaft and passed to the propeller.
notes.example: Like a spring released after being squeezed, driving the plunger back out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Power Stroke”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: As the piston moves through the TDC position at the end of the compression stroke and starts down on the power stroke, it is pushed downward by the rapid expansion of the burning gases within the cylinder head

notes.front: What happens on the exhaust stroke?
notes.back: The rising piston pushes the burned gases out through the exhaust port.
notes.explanation: The fast-leaving gases lower cylinder pressure, which speeds the fresh charge in as the intake valve begins to open.
notes.example: Like squeezing the used air out of a pump before refilling it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Exhaust Stroke”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: As the piston travels through BDC at the completion of the power stroke and starts upward on the exhaust stroke, it begins to push the burned exhaust gases out the exhaust port.

notes.front: What is valve overlap?
notes.back: The period around TDC, between exhaust and intake strokes, when the intake and exhaust valves are both open.
notes.explanation: It comes from opening the intake early (valve lead) and closing the exhaust late (valve lag).
notes.example: Like a relay baton change, where both runners hold the baton for a moment.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Intake Stroke”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: the intake valve opens before TDC on the exhaust stroke (valve lead), and the closing of the exhaust valve is delayed considerably after the piston has passed TDC and has started the intake stroke (valve lag). This timing is called valve overlap

notes.front: What is the two-stroke cycle?
notes.back: A cycle needing only one upstroke and one downstroke of the piston, completed in one crankshaft revolution.
notes.explanation: Intake and exhaust are accomplished during the same stroke.
notes.example: Like a four-stroke cycle squeezed into half the turns.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Two-Stroke Cycle”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: As the name implies, two-stroke cycle engines require only one upstroke and one down stroke of the piston to complete the required series of events in the cylinder. Thus, the engine completes the operating cycle in one revolution of the crankshaft.

notes.front: What is the rotary cycle?
notes.back: A cycle in which a three-sided rotor turns inside an elliptical housing.
notes.explanation: These engines are used mostly with experimental and light aircraft and have very low vibration.
notes.example: Like a triangular spinning top in an oval chamber, with no pistons going up and down.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Rotary Cycle”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: The rotary cycle has a three-sided rotor that turns inside an elliptical housing, completing three of the four cycles for each revolution.

notes.front: What is the diesel cycle?
notes.back: A cycle that relies on high compression pressures, not a spark, to ignite fuel sprayed into the compressed air.
notes.explanation: The high pressure and temperature in the cylinder make the fuel burn, raising pressure and driving the piston down.
notes.example: Like a four-stroke cycle with the spark plug replaced by very hard squeezing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Diesel Cycle”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: The diesel cycle depends on high compression pressures to provide for the ignition of the air-fuel charge in the cylinder. As air is drawn in the cylinder, it is compressed by a piston and, at maximum pressure, fuel is sprayed in the cylinder.

notes.front: What is piston displacement?
notes.back: The volume the piston displaces as it moves from bottom dead centre to TDC.
notes.explanation: Other factors being equal, the greater the displacement, the greater the maximum horsepower.
notes.example: Like the volume a syringe plunger sweeps from one end of its travel to the other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Displacement”, p. 1-28
notes.evidence: When a piston moves from BDC to TDC, it displaces a specific volume. The volume displaced by the piston is known as piston displacement

notes.front: What is an engine’s compression ratio?
notes.back: The cylinder volume with the piston at the bottom of the stroke compared with the volume with it at the top.
notes.explanation: It is a controlling factor in maximum horsepower, limited by fuel grades and the speeds and manifold pressures needed for takeoff.
notes.example: Like squeezing a pump full of air into a tenth of its space: that is 10:1.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Ratio”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: The compression ratio of an engine is a comparison of the volume of space in a cylinder when the piston is at the bottom of the stroke to the volume of space when the piston is at the top of the stroke.

notes.front: What is indicated horsepower (IHP)?
notes.back: The power developed in the combustion chambers, calculated from actual cylinder pressure, without allowing for friction losses.
notes.explanation: It is the theoretical power of a frictionless engine.
notes.example: Like gross pay, before anything is deducted.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Indicated Horsepower”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: Indicated horsepower is the power developed in the combustion chambers without reference to friction losses within the engine. This horsepower is calculated as a function of the actual cylinder pressure recorded during engine operation.

notes.front: What is brake horsepower (BHP)?
notes.back: The power delivered to the propeller for useful work.
notes.explanation: The horsepower lost to friction is subtracted from IHP to arrive at it.
notes.example: Like take-home pay, after the deductions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Brake Horsepower”, p. 1-31
notes.evidence: The total horsepower lost in overcoming friction must be subtracted from the indicated horsepower to arrive at the actual horsepower delivered to the propeller. The power delivered to the propeller for useful work is known as brake horsepower (bhp).

notes.front: What is friction horsepower?
notes.back: IHP minus BHP: the power used overcoming friction, drawing in fuel, expelling exhaust and driving pumps and accessories.
notes.explanation: It is the gap between what the cylinders develop and what reaches the propeller.
notes.example: Like the deductions between gross pay and take-home pay.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Friction Horsepower”, p. 1-32
notes.evidence: Friction horsepower is the indicated horsepower minus brake horsepower. It is the horsepower used by an engine in overcoming the friction of moving parts, drawing in fuel, expelling exhaust, driving oil and fuel pumps, and other engine accessories.

notes.front: What is indicated mean effective pressure (MEP)?
notes.back: The average cylinder pressure that, applied steadily through the power stroke, would do the same work as the actual varying pressure.
notes.explanation: Cylinder pressure varies through the cycle, so an average is computed for use in the IHP calculation.
notes.example: Like an average speed that covers the same distance in the same time as the real stop-start drive.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Indicated Horsepower”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: This average pressure, if applied steadily during the time of the power stroke, would do the same amount of work as the varying pressure during the same period. This average pressure is known as indicated mean effective pressure

notes.front: What is thrust horsepower (THP)?
notes.back: The result of the engine and propeller working together; it would equal BHP only with a 100 percent efficient propeller.
notes.explanation: Propeller efficiency varies with engine speed, attitude, altitude, temperature and airspeed, so the two are never equal.
notes.example: Like the part of a rower’s effort that actually moves the boat, after the oars waste some.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Thrust Horsepower”, p. 1-33
notes.evidence: Thrust horsepower can be considered the result of the engine and the propeller working together. If a propeller could be designed to be 100 percent efficient, the thrust and the bph would be the same.

notes.front: What is mechanical efficiency?
notes.back: The ratio showing how much of the power developed in the cylinders reaches the output shaft: BHP compared with IHP.
notes.explanation: Friction within the engine itself is the factor with the greatest effect on it.
notes.example: Like the share of gross pay that becomes take-home pay.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Mechanical Efficiency”, p. 1-35
notes.evidence: Mechanical efficiency is the ratio that shows how much of the power developed by the expanding gases in the cylinder is actually delivered to the output shaft. It is a comparison between the bhp and the ihp.

notes.front: What is volumetric efficiency?
notes.back: The volume of charge taken in, corrected for temperature and pressure, compared with the engine’s total piston displacement.
notes.explanation: Standard sea-level pressure and temperature are the reference, so the comparison needs correcting to them.
notes.example: Like how full a jug gets each time you dip it, compared with its size.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Volumetric Efficiency”, p. 1-35
notes.evidence: It is a comparison of the volume of air-fuel charge (corrected for temperature and pressure) inducted into the cylinders to the total piston displacement of the engine.

notes.front: What is propulsive efficiency?
notes.back: For a propeller, the ratio of THP to BHP.
notes.explanation: The propeller absorbs BHP and converts it into thrust horsepower, wasting some power in the process.
notes.example: Like the share of pedalling effort that actually moves the bicycle forward.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Propulsive Efficiency”, p. 1-36
notes.evidence: propulsive efficiency (in this case, propeller efficiency) is the ratio of thrust hp to bhp.

notes.front: What is specific fuel consumption (SFC) for a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: Fuel flow in pounds per hour divided by BHP.
notes.explanation: It is usually the basic parameter for describing the fuel economy of aircraft engines.
notes.example: Like fuel used per unit of work done, rather than per hour.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Fuel Economy”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: Specific fuel consumption for gas turbines is the fuel flow measured in (lb/hr) divided by thrust (lb), and for reciprocating engines the fuel flow (lb/hr) divided by brake horsepower.

notes.front: In normal combustion, what is a flame front?
notes.back: The edge of burning that starts at each spark plug and moves across the chamber in a more or less wavelike form.
notes.explanation: In normal combustion the mixture burns progressively at a fairly uniform rate across the chamber.
notes.example: Like ripples spreading from a stone dropped in a pond.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Combustion Process”, p. 10-29
notes.evidence: The flame fronts start at each spark plug and burn in more or less wavelike forms.

notes.front: What is detonation?
notes.back: The spontaneous combustion of the unburned charge ahead of the flame fronts after ignition.
notes.explanation: It occurs when the total compression on the remaining unburned gases exceeds their critical point.
notes.example: Like a fire that suddenly flashes across a room instead of spreading steadily.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Detonation”, p. 10-29
notes.evidence: Detonation is the spontaneous combustion of the unburned charge ahead of the flame fronts after ignition of the charge.

notes.front: What is pre-ignition?
notes.back: Combustion in the cylinder before the timed spark jumps across the spark plug terminals.
notes.explanation: It can often be traced to carbon or other deposits that cause local hot spots.
notes.example: Like a starting pistol that goes off before the starter pulls the trigger.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pre-Ignition”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: Pre-ignition, as the name implies, means that combustion takes place within the cylinder before the timed spark jumps across the spark plug terminals.

notes.front: What is backfiring?
notes.back: An explosion in the induction system when a slow-burning lean charge, still alight in the cylinder, ignites it as the intake valve opens.
notes.explanation: An extremely lean mixture burns so slowly that combustion is not complete at the end of the exhaust stroke.
notes.example: Like a fire creeping back up a fuel line to its source.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Backfiring”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: The flame lingers in the cylinder and then ignites the contents in the intake manifold or the induction system when the intake valve opens. This causes an explosion known as backfiring

notes.front: What is afterfiring?
notes.back: An explosion in the exhaust system when unburned fuel in the exhaust gases mixes with outside air and ignites.
notes.explanation: Overly rich mixtures are slow burning, so charges of unburned fuel leave with the exhaust.
notes.example: Like leftover fuel catching light in the tailpipe after the engine has passed it on.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Afterfiring”, p. 10-31
notes.evidence: Afterfiring, sometimes called afterburning, often results when the air-fuel mixture is too rich. Overly rich mixtures are also slow burning; therefore, charges of unburned fuel are present in the exhausted gases. Air from outside the exhaust stacks mixes with this unburned fuel that ignites. This causes an explosion in the exhaust system.

notes.front: What is hydraulic lock?
notes.back: Liquid drained into a lower cylinder that stops the piston near top centre on compression, because the liquid cannot be compressed.
notes.explanation: Oil or fuel drains into the lower cylinders or intake pipes of a radial engine left shut down beyond a few minutes.
notes.example: Like trying to close a syringe that is full of water with its tip blocked.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hydraulic Lock”, p. 10-25
notes.evidence: As the piston approaches top center of the compression stroke (both valves closed), this liquid being incompressible, stops piston movement.

notes.front: What is an engine overhaul, and when is it due?
notes.back: Taking the engine out of service to recondition it, at a total time in service set by its manufacturer.
notes.explanation: The interval is usually counted in hours of operation and, depending on how the engine is used, it can be mandatory.
notes.example: Like a car’s major service at a set mileage, but going deep enough to recondition the worn engine parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Overhaul”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Each engine manufacturer sets a total time in service when the engine should be removed from service and overhauled.

notes.front: What is pre-oiling an engine?
notes.back: Before first start after overhaul or major maintenance, cranking with the spark plugs out until oil pressure shows, to remove trapped air.
notes.explanation: Air can be trapped in some of the oil passages and must be removed before the first start.
notes.example: Like priming a garden pump before expecting water from it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pre-Oiling”, p. 10-25
notes.evidence: Engines that have undergone overhaul or major maintenance can have air trapped in some of the oil passages that must be removed before the first start. This is done by pre-oiling the engine by cranking, with the spark plugs removed

notes.front: What is valve blow-by, and how is it noticed?
notes.back: Leakage past a valve, heard as a hissing or whistle when the propeller is pulled through or the engine is turned.
notes.explanation: It must be corrected immediately to prevent valve failure and possible engine failure.
notes.example: Like air hissing past a tyre valve that does not quite seat.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Blow-By”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: Valve blow-by is indicated by a hissing or whistle when pulling the propeller through prior to starting the engine, when turning the engine with the starter

notes.front: What is a top overhaul?
notes.back: An overhaul of the parts on top of the crankcase, reconditioning the cylinders without completely dismantling the engine.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls the name a little misleading: it is really an engine repair, not a true overhaul.
notes.example: Like refurbishing the upstairs of a house without touching the foundations.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Top Overhaul”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Reciprocating piston aircraft engines can be repaired by a top overhaul. This means an overhaul of those parts on top of the crankcase, without completely dismantling the engine.

notes.front: What is a major overhaul?
notes.back: The complete reconditioning of the powerplant, including disassembly of the crankcase.
notes.explanation: Every part is inspected and overhauled to the manufacturer’s tolerances, and all accessories are removed, overhauled and tested.
notes.example: Like rebuilding a house down to its foundations rather than redecorating one floor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Major Overhaul & Major Repairs”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Major overhaul consists of the complete reconditioning of the powerplant. A reciprocating engine would require that the crankcase be disassembled

notes.front: What is brinelling?
notes.back: One or more indentations on bearing races, usually from high static loads or force during installation or removal.
notes.explanation: The dents are rounded or spherical because they are the impressions of the bearing’s balls or rollers.
notes.example: Like dimples pressed into a track by marbles when a heavy weight stands on it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Brinelling—one or more indentations on bearing races, usually caused by high static loads or application of force during installation or removal. Indentations are rounded or spherical due to the impression left by the contacting balls or rollers of the bearing.

notes.front: What is galling?
notes.back: A severe form of chafing or fretting in which metal transfers from one part to another.
notes.explanation: It usually comes from slight movement of mated parts that have limited relative motion under high loads.
notes.example: Like two surfaces rubbing so hard under load that bits of one weld onto the other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Galling—a severe condition of chafing or fretting in which a transfer of metal from one part to another occurs. It is usually caused by a slight movement of mated parts having limited relative motion and under high loads.

notes.front: What is scoring?
notes.back: A series of deep scratches in a part.
notes.explanation: It is caused by foreign particles between moving parts, or by careless assembly or disassembly techniques.
notes.example: Like the grooves grit leaves when dragged between two sliding surfaces.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Scoring—a series of deep scratches caused by foreign particles between moving parts or careless assembly or disassembly techniques.

notes.front: What is a corrosion-preventive mixture?
notes.back: Engine oil blended with a light corrosion preventive compound, used to preserve an engine.
notes.explanation: The light compound blends readily with engine oil when the mixture is heated to the proper temperature.
notes.example: Like engine oil with a protective wax dissolved in it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Corrosion-Preventive Compounds”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: The type mixed with engine oil to form a corrosion-preventive mixture is a relatively light compound that readily blends with engine oil when the mixture is heated to the proper temperature.

notes.front: What is a desiccant?
notes.back: A substance that absorbs moisture from the air in useful quantities, such as silica gel, used to dehydrate a stored engine.
notes.explanation: Silica gel is ideal because it does not dissolve when saturated.
notes.example: Like the little sachets packed in a new pair of shoes to keep them dry.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dehydrating Agents”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: There are a number of substances (referred to as desiccants) that can absorb moisture from the atmosphere in sufficient quantities to be useful as dehydrators. One of these is silica gel.

notes.front: What is an engine shipping container?
notes.back: A wooden shipping case or pressurised metal container in which an engine, sealed in a plastic or foil envelope, is packed.
notes.explanation: Silica gel inside dehydrates the enclosed air, and a humidity indicator is visible through a window.
notes.example: Like a sealed crate with a moisture gauge you can read without opening it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Shipping Containers”, p. 8-21
notes.evidence: For protection, engines are sealed in plastic or foil envelopes and can be packed in a wooden shipping case or in pressurized metal containers.

notes.front: What is depreservation of an engine?
notes.back: Removing a stored engine’s preservation materials and inspecting it before it is installed in an aircraft.
notes.explanation: It involves more than taking the engine out of its container and bolting it to the aircraft.
notes.example: Like unpacking and checking over a mothballed machine before running it again.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Depreservation of an Engine”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: An aircraft engine and its accessories that have been in storage must undergo careful depreservation and inspection before they may be installed in an aircraft.

notes.front: How are light-sport aircraft engines classified?
notes.back: By operating cycle, cylinder arrangement, and air or water cooling.
notes.explanation: They range from two-cylinder inline two-strokes to horizontally opposed engines of two to six cylinders.
notes.example: Like ordinary aircraft engines in miniature, including two-strokes seldom seen on certificated aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Light-Sport Aircraft Engines”, p. 11-3
notes.evidence: Light-sport/ultralight aircraft engines can be classified by several methods, such as by operating cycles, cylinder arrangement, and air- or water-cooled.

notes.front: What is the two-cycle Rotax engine, such as the 447 or 503?
notes.back: A two-cylinder inline two-stroke engine, piston ported, with air-cooled cylinder heads and cylinders.
notes.explanation: It comes in a fan-cooled or free air-cooled version.
notes.example: Like a large two-stroke motorcycle engine adapted to turn a propeller.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Two-Cycle, Two Cylinder Rotax Engine”, p. 11-3
notes.evidence: The two cylinder, inline two-stroke engine, which is piston ported with air-cooled cylinder heads and cylinders, is available in a fan or free air-cooled version.

notes.front: What is the Rotax 912?
notes.back: A four-cylinder, four-stroke, horizontally opposed Rotax engine used in light-sport aircraft.
notes.explanation: It is a typical example of the opposed four-strokes used in light-sport and experimental aircraft.
notes.example: Like a small flat-four aircraft engine, sized for light aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Rotax 912/914”, p. 11-5
notes.evidence: Rotax 912/914 Figure 11-6 shows a typical four cylinder, four-stroke Rotax horizontally opposed engine.

notes.front: How are an engine’s reliability and durability each measured?
notes.back: Reliability as the mean time between failures; durability as the mean time between overhauls.
notes.explanation: The two are usually treated as identical factors because it is hard to mention one without the other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Durability & Reliability”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: Simply put, reliability is measured as the mean time between failures, while durability is measured as the mean time between overhauls.

notes.front: Besides cylinder arrangement, how else may reciprocating engines be classified?
notes.back: By method of cooling: liquid cooled or air cooled.
notes.explanation: All piston engines in fact shed excess heat to the surrounding air; the difference is whether a coolant carries it there.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Types of Engines”, p. 1-3
notes.evidence: Reciprocating engines may be classified according to the cylinder arrangement (inline, V-type, radial, and opposed) or according to the method of cooling (liquid cooled or air cooled).

notes.front: What two advantages does an inline engine gain when mounted inverted?
notes.back: A shorter landing gear and greater pilot visibility.
notes.explanation: With the cylinders below the crankshaft, the engine sits lower and out of the pilot’s line of sight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Inline Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: When mounted with the cylinders in an inverted position, it offers the added advantages of a shorter landing gear and greater pilot visibility.

notes.front: What are two advantages of the opposed-type engine?
notes.back: Any two: low weight-to-horsepower ratio; narrow silhouette suiting wing installation; low vibration.
notes.explanation: The narrow silhouette is what makes it ideal for horizontal installation on the wings of twin-engine aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Opposed or O-Type Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: The opposed-type engine has a low weight-to-horsepower ratio, and its narrow silhouette makes it ideal for horizontal installation on the aircraft wings (twin engine applications). Another advantage is its low vibration characteristics.

notes.front: What does the number in a V-type engine designation such as V-1710 give?
notes.back: The piston displacement in cubic inches.
notes.explanation: The designation is a V, a dash and the displacement.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “V-Type Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: The engines are designated by a V followed by a dash and the piston displacement in cubic inches. For example, V-1710.

notes.front: What is a double-row radial?
notes.back: A radial engine with two rows of seven or nine cylinders, one row in front of the other.
notes.explanation: Adding a second row adds cylinders without widening the engine’s circle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Radial Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: Some radial engines have two rows of seven or nine cylinders arranged radially about the crankcase, one in front of the other. These are called double-row radials.

notes.front: What material is generally used for crankcases, and why?
notes.back: Cast or forged aluminium alloy, because it is light and strong.
notes.explanation: The crankcase must be rigid enough to keep the crankshaft and its bearings aligned without adding weight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankcase Section”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: Cast or forged aluminum alloy is generally used for crankcase construction because it is light and strong.

notes.front: What does a slight leak at an intake pipe slip joint do to idling on an un-supercharged engine?
notes.back: The engine may idle fast because the mixture is slightly leaned; a large leak may stop it idling at all.
notes.explanation: Outside pressure is higher than inside at idle, so air leaks in.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankcase Section”, p. 1-6
notes.evidence: If the slip joint connection has a slight leakage, the engine may idle fast due to a slight leaning of the mixture. If the leak is quite large, it may not idle at all.

notes.front: Why is the crankcase nose section larger on engines of 1,000 to 2,500 hp?
notes.back: To house the propeller reduction gears.
notes.explanation: A direct-drive, low-powered engine can use a tapered nose because no reduction gears need housing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankcase Section”, p. 1-6
notes.evidence: The crankcase nose section on engines that develop from 1,000 to 2,500 hp is usually larger to house reduction gears and sometimes ribbed to get as much strength as possible.

notes.front: In accessory gear trains, what are spur-type gears generally used for?
notes.back: Driving the heavier loaded accessories, or those needing the least play or backlash.
notes.explanation: Bevel gears, by contrast, allow short stub shafts to be set at angles to reach the mounting pads.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Accessory Gear Trains”, p. 1-7
notes.evidence: Spur-type gears are generally used to drive the heavier loaded accessories or those requiring the least play or backlash in the gear train.

notes.front: Which part of a crankshaft is supported by, and rotates in, a main bearing?
notes.back: The journal.
notes.explanation: It is the crankshaft’s centre of rotation and is surface-hardened to reduce wear.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshafts”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: The journal is supported by, and rotates in, a main bearing. It serves as the center of rotation of the crankshaft. It is surfacehardened to reduce wear.

notes.front: Which part of a crankshaft does the connecting rod attach to?
notes.back: The crankpin, which is off-centre from the main journals and often called the throw.
notes.explanation: Two crank cheeks and a crankpin make a throw.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshafts”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: The crankpin is the section to which the connecting rod is attached. It is off-center from the main journals and is often called the throw.

notes.front: What does the crank cheek connect?
notes.back: The crankpin to the main journal.
notes.explanation: In some designs it extends beyond the journal to carry a flyweight that balances the crankshaft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshafts”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: The crank cheek connects the crankpin to the main journal. In some designs, the cheek extends beyond the journal and carries a flyweight to balance the crankshaft.

notes.front: Why is the crankpin usually hollow?
notes.back: It reduces crankshaft weight and gives a passage for lubricating oil.
notes.explanation: On early engines the hollow also collected sludge, which newer engines no longer need thanks to ashless dispersant oils.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshafts”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: The crankpin is usually hollow. This reduces the total weight of the crankshaft and provides a passage for the transfer of lubricating oil.

notes.front: Which crankshaft type is used in a single-row radial engine?
notes.back: The single-throw, or 360°, crankshaft, with a main bearing at each end.
notes.explanation: A radial engine has one throw for each row of cylinders.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshafts”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: The simplest crankshaft is the single-throw or 360° type. This type is used in a single-row radial engine. It can be constructed in one or two pieces. Two main bearings (one on each end) are provided

notes.front: Which engines use the double-throw, or 180°, crankshaft?
notes.back: Double-row radial engines.
notes.explanation: In a radial engine one throw is provided for each row of cylinders.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshafts”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: The double-throw or 180° crankshaft is used on doublerow radial engines. In the radial-type engine, one throw is provided for each row of cylinders.

notes.front: When is a crankshaft statically balanced, and how is this checked?
notes.back: When crankpins, cheeks and flyweights balance about the axis of rotation; it is checked on two knife edges.
notes.explanation: If the shaft tends to turn toward any one position on the knife edges, it is out of static balance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshaft Balance”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: A crankshaft is statically balanced when the weight of the entire assembly of crankpins, crank cheeks, and flyweights is balanced around the axis of rotation. When checked for static balance, it is placed on two knife edges.

notes.front: When is a crankshaft dynamically balanced?
notes.back: When the forces of crankshaft rotation and power impulses balance within themselves, so little or no vibration results in operation.
notes.explanation: Excessive vibration causes fatigue failure and rapid wear, and an unbalanced crankshaft is one cause.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dynamic Dampers”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: A crankshaft is dynamically balanced when all the forces created by crankshaft rotation and power impulses are balanced within themselves so that little or no vibration is produced when the engine is operating.

notes.front: How does a dynamic damper reduce vibration?
notes.back: Its pendulum frequency matches the power impulses, and it oscillates out of time with the crankshaft vibration.
notes.explanation: Swinging out of time with the vibration is what cancels much of it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dynamic Dampers”, p. 1-9
notes.evidence: frequency corresponds to the frequency of the power impulses of the engine. When the vibration frequency of the crankshaft occurs, the pendulum oscillates out of time with the crankshaft vibration, thus reducing vibration to a minimum.

notes.front: The four types of connecting-rod assembly are plain, fork and blade, master and articulated, and {{c1::split-type}}.
notes.back: split-type
notes.explanation: Which type an engine uses depends on its cylinder arrangement.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Connecting Rods”, p. 1-9
notes.evidence: There are four types of connecting-rod assemblies [Figure 1-11]: 1. Plain. 2. Fork and blade. 3. Master and articulated. 4. Split-type.

notes.front: How many master rods and articulated rods does an 18-cylinder, two-row radial have?
notes.back: Two master rods and 16 articulated rods.
notes.explanation: There is one master rod in each row; every other piston hangs on an articulated rod.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Master-and-Articulated Rod Assembly”, p. 1-9
notes.evidence: In an 18-cylinder engine, which has two rows of cylinders, there are two master rods and 16 articulated rods.

notes.front: Why do the pistons on articulated rods not move equal amounts for a given crank movement?
notes.back: The knuckle pins travel in elliptical paths, giving the link rods varying angularity.
notes.explanation: The knuckle pin centres do not coincide with the crankpin centre.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Master-and-Articulated Rod Assembly”, p. 1-10
notes.evidence: Because of the varying angularity of the link rods and the elliptical motion of the knuckle pins, all pistons do not move an equal amount in each cylinder for a given number of degrees of crank throw movement.

notes.front: What is a cam ground piston?
notes.back: A piston that is oval when cold, larger across the pin, and becomes round at operating temperature.
notes.explanation: The part in line with the pin has more mass and expands more, which reduces cocking or slap during warm-up.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pistons”, p. 1-12
notes.evidence: At low temperatures, the piston is oval shaped and, when it warms to operating temperature, it becomes round. This process reduces the tendency of the piston to cock or slap in the cylinder during warm up.

notes.front: On engines whose rotating and reciprocating assembly is balanced, pistons must weigh within {{c1::one-fourth ounce}} of each other.
notes.back: one-fourth ounce
notes.explanation: A new piston must match the one removed; weight can be filed off but never added by welding or plating.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Repairs”, p. 10-17
notes.evidence: On engines where the entire rotating and reciprocating assembly is balanced, the pistons must weigh within one-fourth ounce of each other.

notes.front: Why is the modern piston pin called full-floating?
notes.back: It is free to rotate in both the piston and the connecting rod’s piston-pin bearing.
notes.explanation: Neither end is clamped, so the pin must be held in place by other means.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Pin”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The piston pin used in modern aircraft engines is the full-floating type, so called because the pin is free to rotate in both the piston and in the connecting rod piston-pin bearing.

notes.front: Why is a plug of soft aluminium fitted in the end of a piston pin?
notes.back: It gives a good bearing surface against the cylinder wall, so the pin ends do not score it.
notes.explanation: A floating pin must be held in place to keep its ends off the cylinder walls.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Pin”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The piston pin must be held in place to prevent the pin ends from scoring the cylinder walls. A plug of relatively soft aluminum in the pin end provides a good bearing surface against the cylinder wall.

notes.front: What rule applies to chrome-plated piston rings?
notes.back: Use them with steel cylinder walls; never use chrome rings on chrome cylinders.
notes.explanation: Chrome-plated mild steel rings suit the top groove because they better withstand its high temperatures.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Ring Construction”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: Chrome rings must be used with steel cylinder walls. Never use chrome rings on chrome cylinders.

notes.front: What does the tapered face of a wedge-section compression ring do?
notes.back: It presents a narrow bearing edge to the cylinder wall, reducing friction and sealing better.
notes.explanation: The alternative cross-section is rectangular.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Ring”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The cross-section of the ring is either rectangular or wedge shaped with a tapered face. The tapered face presents a narrow bearing edge to the cylinder wall, which helps to reduce friction and provide better sealing.

notes.front: What are two problems that carbon from excess oil can cause?
notes.back: Any two: sticking valves and rings; spark plug misfiring; detonation, pre-ignition or excessive oil consumption.
notes.explanation: The carbon comes from oil burning in the combustion chamber when the oil film is too thick.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Oil Control Rings”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: This carbon can cause the valves and piston rings to stick if it enters the ring grooves or valve guides. In addition, the carbon can cause spark plug misfiring as well as detonation, pre-ignition, or excessive oil consumption.

notes.front: How is a gastight joint made between an aluminium cylinder head and a steel barrel?
notes.back: The head is heated and screwed onto the chilled barrel; as temperatures equalise, the joint tightens.
notes.explanation: The head contracts as it cools while the barrel expands as it warms.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinders”, p. 1-14
notes.evidence: At assembly, the cylinder head is expanded by heating and then screwed down on the cylinder barrel, which has been chilled. When the head cools and contracts and the barrel warms up and expands, a gastight joint results.

notes.front: Which part of the cylinder head gets more cooling-fin area, and why?
notes.back: The exhaust valve region, because it is the hottest part of the internal surface.
notes.explanation: Temperatures differ across the head, so fin area is matched to the heat.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Heads”, p. 1-15
notes.evidence: The exhaust valve region is the hottest part of the internal surface; therefore, more fin area is provided around the outside of the cylinder in this section.

notes.front: How is a cylinder barrel nitrided?
notes.back: The very hot steel is exposed to ammonia or cyanide gas and absorbs nitrogen, forming hard iron nitrides on the surface.
notes.explanation: The hardening penetrates only a few thousandths of an inch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Barrels”, p. 1-15
notes.evidence: This hardening is usually done by exposing the steel to ammonia or cyanide gas while the steel is very hot. The steel soaks up nitrogen from the gas, which forms iron nitrides on the exposed surface.

notes.front: Why are some cylinder barrels choked?
notes.back: They are made smaller in diameter at the top to allow for heat expansion and wear.
notes.explanation: The top of the cylinder runs hotter than the bottom, so it expands more.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Barrels”, p. 1-15
notes.evidence: Some engine cylinder barrels are choked at the top, or they are smaller in diameter to allow for heat expansion and wear.

notes.front: Which end of an engine is always its front?
notes.back: The propeller shaft end, however the engine is mounted in the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The accessory end is always the rear.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Numbering”, p. 1-15
notes.evidence: The propeller shaft end of the engine is always the front end, and the accessory end is the rear end, regardless of how the engine is mounted in an aircraft.

notes.front: Is cylinder numbering of opposed engines standard?
notes.back: No: some manufacturers number from the rear, others from the front; check the engine manual.
notes.explanation: Only the manufacturer’s manual settles which system an engine uses.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Numbering”, p. 1-15
notes.evidence: The numbering of opposed engine cylinders is by no means standard. Some manufacturers number their cylinders from the rear and others from the front of the engine. Always refer to the appropriate engine manual

notes.front: How are single-row radial cylinders numbered?
notes.back: Clockwise as viewed from the rear, with No. 1 the top cylinder.
notes.explanation: Double-row engines use the same system across both rows.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Numbering”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: Single-row radial engine cylinders are numbered clockwise when viewed from the rear. Cylinder No. 1 is the top cylinder.

notes.front: On a single-row radial, in what pattern do the cylinders fire?
notes.back: All odd-numbered cylinders in numerical succession, then all even-numbered cylinders in succession.
notes.explanation: For nine cylinders that gives 1-3-5-7-9-2-4-6-8.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Single-Row Radial Engines”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: On a single-row radial engine, all the odd-numbered cylinders fire in numerical succession; then, the even numbered cylinders fire in numerical succession.

notes.front: What rule gives the firing order of a 14-cylinder double-row radial?
notes.back: From any cylinder, add 9 or subtract 5, whichever gives an answer from 1 to 14.
notes.explanation: 9 and 5 are called the firing order numbers for this engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Double-Row Radial Engines”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: An easy method for computing the firing order of a 14-cylinder, double-row radial engine is to start with any number from 1 to 14 and add 9 or subtract 5 (these are called the firing order numbers), whichever gives an answer between 1 and 14, inclusive.

notes.front: What are the firing order numbers of an 18-cylinder double-row radial?
notes.back: 11 and 7: add 11 or subtract 7, staying between 1 and 18.
notes.explanation: The rule works the same way as for the 14-cylinder engine, with different numbers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Firing Order”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: The firing order numbers of an 18-cylinder, double-row radial engine are 11 and 7; that is, begin with any number from 1 to 18 and add 11 or subtract 7.

notes.front: Why can intake valves be made of chromic-nickel steel while exhaust valves need nichrome, silchrome or cobalt-chromium steel?
notes.back: Intake valves run cooler; the exhaust valve alloys are much more heat resistant.
notes.explanation: Valves face high temperatures, corrosion and operating stresses.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Construction”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: Because intake valves operate at lower temperatures than exhaust valves, they can be made of chromic-nickel steel. Exhaust valves are usually made of nichrome, silchrome, or cobalt-chromium steel because these materials are much more heat resistant.

notes.front: How is an intake valve often identified?
notes.back: By a flat milled on its tip.
notes.explanation: Similar intake and exhaust valves are not interchangeable, as their faces are of different material.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Construction”, p. 1-18
notes.evidence: Although these valves are similar, they are not interchangeable since the faces of the valves are constructed of different material. The intake valve usually has a flat milled on the tip to identify it.

notes.front: What happens if the sodium in a sodium-filled valve is exposed to outside air?
notes.back: Fire or explosion, with possible personal injury.
notes.explanation: So a sodium-filled valve must never be cut open or treated in a way that may rupture it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Construction”, p. 1-18
notes.evidence: Exposure of the sodium in these valves to the outside air results in fire or explosion with possible personal injury.

notes.front: What two things does the shape of the cam lobes determine?
notes.back: Valve lift and valve duration.
notes.explanation: Lift is how far the valve leaves its seat; duration is how long it is held open.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Operating Mechanism”, p. 1-18
notes.evidence: The valve lift (distance that the valve is lifted off its seat) and the valve duration (length of time the valve is held open) are both determined by the shape of the cam lobes.

notes.front: Which way does a cam ring turn if driven through teeth on its outside?
notes.back: In the direction of crankshaft rotation; driven from the inside, it turns opposite.
notes.explanation: The drive arrangement and lobe spacing together set the valve timing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cam Rings”, p. 1-19
notes.evidence: If the reduction gear meshes with the teeth on the outside of the ring, the cam turns in the direction of rotation of the crankshaft. If the ring is driven from the inside, the cam turns in the opposite direction from the crankshaft.

notes.front: At what speed does an opposed engine’s camshaft turn?
notes.back: Always at one-half crankshaft speed.
notes.explanation: The cam gear is twice the size of the crankshaft gear.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Camshaft”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: The camshaft always rotates at one-half the crankshaft speed.

notes.front: At overhaul, how are hydraulic valve lifters adjusted?
notes.back: Assembled dry, clearances checked, and adjustments usually made with push rods of different lengths.
