notes.explanation: Clearance anywhere between the minimum and maximum is acceptable, but about halfway is desired.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hydraulic Valve Tappets/Lifters”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Hydraulic valve lifters are normally adjusted at the time of overhaul. They are assembled dry (no lubrication), clearances checked, and adjustments are usually made by using push rods of different lengths.

notes.front: What are two advantages of hydraulic valve lifters over the screw adjustment type?
notes.back: Any two: less maintenance; better lubrication; quieter operation.
notes.explanation: They also compensate automatically for expansion and contraction in the valve train.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hydraulic Valve Tappets/Lifters”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Hydraulic valve lifters require less maintenance, are better lubricated, and operate more quietly than the screw adjustment type.

notes.front: When push rods are reinstalled, what two rules apply?
notes.back: Install each in its original location, and never turn one end to end.
notes.explanation: Their ball ends are usually worn to fit the sockets they have been working in.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Installation”, p. 10-43
notes.evidence: Remember that the push rods must be installed in their original locations and must not be turned end to end.

notes.front: How many springs close each valve?
notes.back: Two or three helical springs, one inside the other.
notes.explanation: A single spring would vibrate or surge at certain speeds.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Springs”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Each valve is closed by two or three helical springs. If a single spring were used, it would vibrate or surge at certain speeds.

notes.front: How do two or more springs per valve prevent spring surge?
notes.back: Each spring vibrates at a different engine speed, so spring-surge vibrations are rapidly damped.
notes.explanation: Multiple springs also reduce the danger of failure by breakage from heat and metal fatigue.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Springs”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Each spring vibrates at a different engine speed and rapid damping out of all spring-surge vibrations during engine operation results.

notes.front: What is the difference between a radial load and a thrust load on a bearing?
notes.back: A radial load holds a rotating shaft in one position on a radial plane; a thrust load keeps it from moving axially.
notes.explanation: Bearings are required to take one or the other, or a combination.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Bearings”, p. 1-22
notes.evidence: An example of a radial load would be a rotating shaft being held or contained in one position on a radial plane. Thrust load would be the rotating shaft being contained from moving axially along the shafts axis.

notes.front: What do special deep-groove ball bearings do in radial engines?
notes.back: They transmit propeller thrust and radial loads to the engine nose section.
notes.explanation: Ball bearings can accept both radial and thrust loads.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ball Bearings”, p. 1-22
notes.evidence: Special deep-groove ball bearings are used to transmit propeller thrust and radial loads to the engine nose section of radial engines.

notes.front: Where are straight roller bearings used in high-power reciprocating engines?
notes.back: As the crankshaft main bearings.
notes.explanation: Straight roller bearings suit places with radial loads only.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Roller Bearings”, p. 1-22
notes.evidence: Straight roller bearings are used in high power reciprocating aircraft engines for the crankshaft main bearings.

notes.front: What three types of propeller reduction gearing are most commonly used?
notes.back: Spur planetary, bevel planetary, and spur and pinion.
notes.explanation: Lower-powered engines can use the spur and pinion arrangement.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Propeller Reduction Gearing”, p. 1-23
notes.evidence: The three types most commonly used are spur planetary, bevel planetary, and spur and pinion.

notes.front: Which propeller shaft type is used on most modern reciprocating and turboprop engines?
notes.back: The flanged shaft, drilled to take the propeller mounting bolts.
notes.explanation: It is a very common installation on most propeller-driven aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Propeller Shafts”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Flanged propeller shafts are used on most modern reciprocating and turboprop engines. One end of the shaft is flanged with drilled holes to accept the propeller mounting bolts.

notes.front: What are the five events of a four-stroke cycle engine, in order?
notes.back: Intake, compression, ignition, power and exhaust.
notes.explanation: Ignition is an event, not a stroke, so five events fit into four strokes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Operating Principles”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Therefore, the order of the five events of a four stroke cycle engine are intake, compression, ignition, power, and exhaust.

notes.front: In a four-stroke engine, how often does each cylinder fire?
notes.back: Once in every two crankshaft revolutions (720°).
notes.explanation: Four strokes take two full revolutions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Four-Stroke Cycle”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Two complete revolutions of the crankshaft (720°) are required for the four strokes; thus, each cylinder in an engine of this type fires once in every two revolutions of the crankshaft.

notes.front: How far before TDC is the charge ignited?
notes.back: From 20° to 35° before TDC, depending on the engine.
notes.explanation: This ensures complete combustion by the time the piston is slightly past TDC.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Stroke”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: The time of ignition varies from 20° to 35° before TDC, depending upon the requirements of the specific engine to ensure complete combustion of the charge by the time the piston is slightly past the TDC position.

notes.front: Why is thorough scavenging very important?
notes.back: Exhaust products left in the cylinder dilute the incoming air-fuel charge of the next cycle.
notes.explanation: Early exhaust valve opening and valve overlap both help scavenge the cylinder.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Power Stroke”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: Thorough scavenging is very important, because any exhaust products remaining in the cylinder dilute the incoming air-fuel charge at the start of the next cycle.

notes.front: How far past bottom dead centre does the intake valve close, and why?
notes.back: About 50° to 75° past bottom dead centre, letting the momentum of the incoming gases charge the cylinder more fully.
notes.explanation: Too late a closing forces gases back out through the intake valve.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Intake Stroke”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: The intake valve is timed to close about 50° to 75° past BDC on the compression stroke, depending upon the specific engine, to allow the momentum of the incoming gases to charge the cylinder more completely.

notes.front: What are two purposes of valve overlap?
notes.back: Any two: cooling the cylinder internally; increasing the charge induced; aiding scavenging.
notes.explanation: The cool incoming charge circulating through the cylinder is what cools it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Intake Stroke”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: This timing is called valve overlap and is designed to aid in cooling the cylinder internally by circulating the cool incoming air-fuel mixture, to increase the amount of the air-fuel mixture induced into the cylinder, and to aid in scavenging the byproducts of combustion from the cylinder.

notes.front: The {{c1::bore}} of a cylinder is its inside diameter.
notes.back: bore
notes.explanation: Bore and stroke together fix a cylinder’s displacement.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Operating Principles”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: The bore of a cylinder is its inside diameter.

notes.front: Where has the two-stroke-cycle engine re-emerged?
notes.back: In ultralight, light-sport and many experimental aircraft.
notes.explanation: These engines generally need a gear reduction housing between engine and propeller.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Two-Stroke Cycle”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: The two-stroke-cycle engine has re-emerged and is being used in ultra-light, light sport, and many experimental aircraft.

notes.front: Which aircraft engines use a version of the diesel cycle?
notes.back: Water- and air-cooled engines that can run on Jet A fuel (kerosene).
notes.explanation: Diesels exist in both two-stroke and four-stroke forms.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Diesel Cycle”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: Water and air cooled engines that can operate on JET A fuel (kerosene) use a version of the diesel cycle. There are many types of diesel cycles in use including two-stroke and four-stroke diesels.

notes.front: How is an engine’s total piston displacement found?
notes.back: Cylinder cross-section area × stroke × number of cylinders.
notes.explanation: Area times stroke gives one cylinder’s swept volume.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Displacement”, p. 1-28
notes.evidence: The piston displacement of one cylinder may be obtained by multiplying the area of the cross-section of the cylinder by the total distance the piston moves in the cylinder in one stroke. For multicylinder engines, this product is multiplied by the number of cylinders

notes.front: What determines the charge pressure just before ignition?
notes.back: Manifold pressure times the compression ratio.
notes.explanation: Compression magnifies any change in manifold pressure; too high a pressure causes pre-ignition or detonation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Ratio”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: the pressure at the height of compression (just prior to ignition) is determined by manifold pressure times the compression ratio.

notes.front: Why are engines with high compression ratios used?
notes.back: For long-range fuel economy: they turn more heat energy into useful work than low-compression engines.
notes.explanation: Less heat then goes into the cylinder walls, giving cooler running and higher thermal efficiency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Ratio”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: One of the reasons for using engines with high compression ratios is to obtain long-range fuel economy, to convert more heat energy into useful work than is done in engines of low compression ratio.

notes.front: In the indicated horsepower formula, what does N stand for in a four-stroke engine?
notes.back: Power strokes per minute: rpm divided by 2.
notes.explanation: Each cylinder fires once every two revolutions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Indicated Horsepower”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: N = Number of power strokes per minute: 2

notes.front: In the indicated horsepower formula, what does P stand for?
notes.back: Indicated mean effective pressure, in psi.
notes.explanation: P times the piston area gives the force on the piston in pounds.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Indicated Horsepower”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: P = Indicated mean effective pressure, in psi

notes.front: With a Prony brake, how is the torque of the shaft found?
notes.back: Force registered on the scale multiplied by the length of the arm.
notes.explanation: The arm stops the brake collar turning with the shaft, so the scale reads the reacting force.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Brake Horsepower”, p. 1-31
notes.evidence: If the resulting force registered on the scale is multiplied by the length of the arm, the resulting product is the torque exerted by the rotating shaft.

notes.front: How is BHP calculated from torque?
notes.back: 2π × torque × rpm ÷ 33,000.
notes.explanation: Work per revolution is 2π × torque, and multiplying by rpm gives work per minute.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Brake Horsepower”, p. 1-32
notes.evidence: If work per revolution is multiplied by the rpm, the result is work per minute, or power. If the work is expressed in ft-lb per minute, this quantity is divided by 33,000. The result is the brake horsepower of the shaft.

notes.front: On modern aircraft engines, how large may friction horsepower be?
notes.back: As high as 10 to 15 percent of IHP.
notes.explanation: It includes pumping, piston friction and accessory drives.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Friction Horsepower”, p. 1-32
notes.evidence: On modern aircraft engines, this power loss through friction may be as high as 10 to 15 percent of

notes.front: Into which two parts is indicated MEP divided?
notes.back: Brake mean effective pressure, which produces BHP, and friction mean effective pressure, which overcomes internal friction.
notes.explanation: Neither exists physically in the cylinder, but both are useful for rating performance and pressure limits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Friction & Brake Mean Effective Pressures”, p. 1-33
notes.evidence: That portion of IMEP that produces brake horsepower is called brake mean effective pressure (BMEP). The remaining pressure used to overcome internal friction is called friction mean effective pressure (FMEP).

notes.front: How is THP calculated from thrust and aircraft speed?
notes.back: Thrust × aircraft speed in mph, divided by 375.
notes.explanation: 1 hp equals 375 mile-pounds per hour.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Power & Weight”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: One horsepower equals 33,000 ft-lb per minute or 375 milepounds per hour.

notes.front: Of the total heat produced in a reciprocating engine, what share goes to power output and what share leaves through the exhaust?
notes.back: 25 to 30 percent to power output; 40 to 45 percent through the exhaust.
notes.explanation: The rest is lost to cooling (15 to 20 percent) and friction (5 to 10 percent).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Thermal Efficiency”, p. 1-34
notes.evidence: Of the total heat produced, 25 to 30 percent is utilized for power output, 15 to 20 percent is lost in cooling (heat radiated from cylinder head fins), 5 to 10 percent is lost in overcoming friction of moving parts; and 40 to 45 percent is lost through the exhaust.

notes.front: What does the mechanical efficiency of the average aircraft reciprocating engine approach?
notes.back: 90 percent.
notes.explanation: Friction within the engine is the main factor that keeps it below 100.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Mechanical Efficiency”, p. 1-35
notes.evidence: Mechanical efficiency of the average aircraft reciprocating engine approaches 90 percent.

notes.front: At what rpm is an engine’s mechanical efficiency highest?
notes.back: At the rpm at which maximum BHP is developed.
notes.explanation: Friction between moving parts stays practically constant across the speed range.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Mechanical Efficiency”, p. 1-35
notes.evidence: The friction between moving parts in an engine remains practically constant throughout an engine’s speed range. Therefore, the mechanical efficiency of an engine is highest when the engine is running at the rpm at which maximum bhp is developed.

notes.front: Which engines may have a volumetric efficiency greater than 100 percent?
notes.back: Engines with true supercharging (boost above 30.00 inches of mercury).
notes.explanation: Drawing in more than a displacement’s worth of standard-density charge is what exceeding 100 percent means.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Volumetric Efficiency”, p. 1-35
notes.evidence: An engine equipped with true supercharging (boost above 30.00 "Hg) may have a volumetric efficiency greater than 100 percent.

notes.front: What are two factors that decrease volumetric efficiency?
notes.back: Any two, among others: part-throttle operation; long, small-diameter intake pipes; sharp bends in the induction system.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s list also includes high air or cylinder temperatures, incomplete scavenging and improper valve timing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Volumetric Efficiency”, p. 1-35
notes.evidence: Many factors decrease volumetric efficiency, including: • Part-throttle operation; • Long intake pipes of small diameter; • Sharp bends in the induction system;

notes.front: On average, what share of BHP becomes THP?
notes.back: About 80 percent; the other 20 percent is lost in friction and slippage.
notes.explanation: That 80 percent is the propeller’s propulsive efficiency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Propulsive Efficiency”, p. 1-36
notes.evidence: On the average, thrust hp constitutes approximately 80 percent of the bhp. The other 20 percent is lost in friction and slippage.

notes.front: What is SFC called for a reciprocating engine, and for a gas turbine?
notes.back: Brake-specific fuel consumption for a reciprocating engine; thrust-specific fuel consumption for a gas turbine.
notes.explanation: One divides fuel flow by BHP, the other by thrust.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Fuel Economy”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: These are called thrust-specific fuel consumption and brake-specific fuel consumption, respectively.

notes.front: With normal combustion, about how fast does the flame travel?
notes.back: About 100 feet per second.
notes.explanation: Its speed depends on the fuel type, the air-fuel ratio, and the mixture’s pressure and temperature.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Combustion Process”, p. 10-29
notes.evidence: The velocity of the flame travel is influenced by the type of fuel, the ratio of the air-fuel mixture, and the pressure and temperature of the fuel mixture. With normal combustion, the flame travel is about 100 feet/second.

notes.front: At overhaul, what signs show an engine has suffered severe detonation?
notes.back: Dished piston heads, collapsed valve heads, broken ring lands, or eroded valves, pistons or cylinder heads.
notes.explanation: Light to medium detonation gives no flight deck evidence, so teardown is often where it is first found.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Detonation”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: When the engine is overhauled, however, the presence of severe detonation during its operation is indicated by dished piston heads, collapsed valve heads, broken ring lands, or eroded portions of valves, pistons, or cylinder heads.

notes.front: Does light to medium detonation show in the flight deck?
notes.back: No: it causes no noticeable roughness, temperature rise or loss of power.
notes.explanation: So it can be present in takeoff and high-power climb without the crew knowing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Detonation”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: Light to medium detonation does not cause noticeable roughness, temperature increase, or loss of power.

notes.front: How is pre-ignition usually indicated in the flight deck?
notes.back: By engine roughness, backfiring and a sudden rise in cylinder head temperature.
notes.explanation: Unlike light detonation, pre-ignition does show itself to the crew.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pre-Ignition”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: Pre-ignition is usually indicated in the flight deck by engine roughness, backfiring, and by a sudden increase in cylinder head temperature.

notes.front: What is the immediate step to correct pre-ignition?
notes.back: Retard the throttle.
notes.explanation: This cuts the fuel charge and the heat generated; then reduce manifold pressure and enrich the mixture if possible.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pre-Ignition”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: The most obvious method of correcting pre-ignition is to reduce the cylinder temperature. The immediate step is to retard the throttle.

notes.front: Is pre-ignition caused by incorrect ignition timing?
notes.back: No: it is caused by a hot spot in the combustion chamber, from an overheated cylinder or a defect.
notes.explanation: It resembles early spark timing, but the spark is not what fires the charge.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pre-Ignition”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: However, do not confuse pre-ignition with the spark that occurs too early in the cycle. Pre-ignition is caused by a hot spot in the combustion chamber, not by incorrect ignition timing.

notes.front: Why is backfiring seldom the fault of the carburettor?
notes.back: It rarely involves the whole engine; it is practically always limited to one or two cylinders.
notes.explanation: Usually faulty valve clearance or defective injector nozzles make those cylinders run leaner than the rest.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Backfiring”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: A point worth stressing is that backfiring rarely involves the whole engine. Therefore, it is seldom the fault of the carburetor. In practically all cases, backfiring is limited to one or two cylinders.

notes.front: An engine backfires at idle but runs well at medium and high power. What is the most likely cause?
notes.back: An excessively lean idle mixture.
notes.explanation: Proper adjustment of the idle mixture usually cures it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Backfiring”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: In some instances, an engine backfires in the idle range but operates satisfactorily at medium and high power settings. The most likely cause, in this case, is an excessively lean idle mixture.

notes.front: Besides a rich mixture, what else can cause afterfiring?
notes.back: Cylinders not firing, from faulty plugs, defective injection nozzles or incorrect valve clearance.
notes.explanation: Their unburned mixture passes into the exhaust and burns there, which can be mistaken for a rich carburettor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Afterfiring”, p. 10-31
notes.evidence: Afterfiring can also be caused by cylinders that are not firing because of faulty spark plugs, defective fuel-injection nozzles. or incorrect valve clearance.

notes.front: For full compression, what three things in the cylinder must be right?
notes.back: Rings in good condition; valves closing tightly; and valve timing correct.
notes.explanation: A failure at any of these points greatly reduces engine efficiency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression”, p. 10-31
notes.evidence: First, the piston rings must be in good condition to provide maximum sealing during the stroke of the piston. There must be no leakage between the piston and the walls of the combustion chamber. Second, the intake and exhaust valves must close tightly so that there is no loss of compression at these points. notes.front: What does too much valve clearance do to the idle mixture?
notes.back: The overlap period shortens, less air or exhaust is drawn back in, and the idle mixture tends to be too rich.
notes.explanation: The valves open less wide and for a shorter time than they should.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Operational Effect of Valve Clearance”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: Where there is too much valve clearance, the valves do not open as wide or remain open as long as they should. This reduces the overlap period. At idling speed, it affects the air-fuel mixture, since a less-than-normal amount of air or exhaust gases is drawn back into the cylinder

notes.front: What does too little valve clearance do to the idle mixture?
notes.back: The overlap period lengthens, more air or exhaust is drawn back in, and the idle mixture is leaned out.
notes.explanation: The carburettor is set expecting a certain amount of air or exhaust drawn back in at idle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Operational Effect of Valve Clearance”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: When valve clearance is less than it should be, the valve overlap period is lengthened. A greater than normal amount of air, or exhaust gases, is drawn back into the cylinder at idling speeds. As a result, the idle mixture is leaned out at the cylinder.

notes.front: Why must a hydraulic lock never be cleared by pulling the propeller opposite to normal rotation?
notes.back: It pushes the liquid into the intake pipe, risking a lock on the next start.
notes.explanation: The piston would expel the liquid through the open intake instead of out of the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hydraulic Lock”, p. 10-25
notes.evidence: Never attempt to clear the hydraulic lock by pulling the propeller through in the direction opposite to normal rotation. This tends to inject the liquid from the cylinder into the intake pipe

notes.front: How is a hydraulic lock eliminated?
notes.back: Remove the front or rear spark plug of the lower cylinders and pull the propeller through in the direction of rotation.
notes.explanation: The piston then expels the liquid through the plug hole.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hydraulic Lock”, p. 10-25
notes.evidence: To eliminate a lock, remove either the front or rear spark plug of the lower cylinders and pull the propeller through in the direction of rotation. The piston expels any liquid that may be present.

notes.front: What is the optimum warm-up speed range?
notes.back: 1,000 to 1,600 rpm, choosing the speed at which the engine runs smoothest.
notes.explanation: Smooth running shows that all phases of engine operation are most stable.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Warm-Up”, p. 10-25
notes.evidence: Experience has shown that the optimum warm-up speed is from 1,000 to 1,600 rpm.

notes.front: After start, when should oil pressure show, and when must the engine be shut down?
notes.back: It should show within 30 seconds; shut down if it is not normal within 1 minute.
notes.explanation: Instruments are watched throughout warm-up to confirm all is normal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Warm-Up”, p. 10-26
notes.evidence: For example, engine oil pressure should be indicated within 30 seconds after the start. Furthermore, if the oil pressure is not up to or above normal within 1 minute after the engine starts, the engine should be shut down.

notes.front: What does the ground check compare?
notes.back: Power input, measured by manifold pressure, with power output, measured by rpm or torque.
notes.explanation: An engine may produce rated power and still not be working properly; only this comparison reveals it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ground Check”, p. 10-26
notes.evidence: The ground check is performed to evaluate the functioning of the engine by comparing power input, as measured by manifold pressure, with power output, as measured by rpm or torque.

notes.front: In the magneto check, what usually causes a fast rpm drop?
notes.back: Faulty spark plugs or a faulty ignition harness.
notes.explanation: These take effect at once: the cylinder goes dead the instant the switch moves.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ground Check”, p. 10-27
notes.evidence: Fast rpm drop is usually the result of either faulty spark plugs or faulty ignition harness.

notes.front: During the ground check, where must fuel and oil pressure be?
notes.back: Within the established tolerance, the green arc, for the engine.
notes.explanation: The green arc marks the normal operating range.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Fuel Pressure & Oil Pressure Check”, p. 10-27
notes.evidence: Fuel pressure and oil pressure must be within the established tolerance (green arc) for the engine.

notes.front: In the power check, what does excessively low manifold pressure for the rpm usually indicate?
notes.back: Early ignition timing.
notes.explanation: Early ignition can cause detonation and loss of power at takeoff settings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Power Check”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: An excessively low manifold pressure for a particular rpm usually indicates that the ignition timing is early.

notes.front: What is the inevitable result of failing to set a proper idle mixture?
notes.back: Spark plug fouling.
notes.explanation: The common fault is an over-rich idle mixture masked by a high throttle-stop idle speed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Idle Speed & Idle Mixture Checks”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: Plug fouling difficulty is the inevitable result of failure to provide a proper idle mixture setting.

notes.front: How is an engine with an idle cut-off mixture control stopped?
notes.back: Idle at 800–1,000 rpm, move the mixture to idle cut-off, then switch the ignition off after the propeller stops.
notes.explanation: Stopping on the mixture burns the cylinders clear of charge before the ignition is turned off.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Stopping”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: An engine equipped with a carburetor incorporating an idle cutoff mixture control is stopped as follows: 1. Idle the engine by setting the throttle for 800 to 1,000 rpm.

notes.front: When stopping an engine, where is the carburettor air-heater control left, and why?
notes.back: In the cold position, to prevent damage from a backfire.
notes.explanation: Cowl flaps are left open to prevent overheating and protect the ignition system from residual heat.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Stopping”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: Carburetor air-heater control is left in the cold position to prevent damage that may occur from backfire.

notes.front: In the troubleshooting chart for opposed engines, what indicates a mixture too lean?
notes.back: Overheating or backfiring.
notes.explanation: The chart’s remedy is to check the fuel lines for dirt or restrictions and check the fuel supply.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Troubleshooting”, p. 10-36
notes.evidence: Mixture too lean; indicated by overheating or

notes.front: If an engine’s performance is faulty, in which systems may the trouble lie?
notes.back: Ignition, fuel metering, induction, power section, or instrumentation.
notes.explanation: A logical approach using the instrument readings pinpoints the system, then the specific fault.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Troubleshooting”, p. 10-38
notes.evidence: If a fault does exist, it may be assumed that the trouble lies in one of the following systems: 1. Ignition system. 2. Fuel-metering system. 3. Induction system. 4. Power section (valves, cylinders, etc.). 5. Instrumentation.

notes.front: How is a valve that is sticking in its guide released, when correcting blow-by?
notes.back: Place a fibre drift on the rocker arm over the valve stem and strike it several times with a mallet.
notes.explanation: First a compression test locates the faulty cylinder and the valve clearance is checked.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Blow-By”, p. 10-39
notes.evidence: To release the sticking valve, place a fiber drift on the rocker arm immediately over the valve stem and strike the drift several times with a mallet.

notes.front: What usually makes a top overhaul necessary?
notes.back: Valves or piston rings wearing prematurely.
notes.explanation: Many argue that an engine needing this much dismantling should instead get a major overhaul.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Top Overhaul”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: This repair is generally due to valves or piston rings wearing prematurely.

notes.front: When is the major overhaul of a reciprocating engine a major repair that a powerplant mechanic may not approve for return to service?
notes.back: When the engine has an integral supercharger or propeller reduction gearing other than spur-type: splitting its crankcase is then a major repair.
notes.explanation: Section 65.87 of the regulations lets a powerplant mechanic approve for return to service only work that excludes major repairs, so such an overhaul needs someone with wider authority.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 43, appendix A, paragraph (b)(2) (eCFR, current)
notes.evidence: Separation or disassembly of a crankcase or crankshaft of a reciprocating engine equipped with an integral supercharger.

notes.front: A complete overhaul has ten steps, beginning with receiving inspection and ending with {{c1::testing and break in}}.
notes.back: testing and break in
notes.explanation: The inspection phases in between are the most precise and most important.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Overhaul”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: A complete overhaul process includes the following ten steps: receiving inspection; disassembly; visual inspection; cleaning; structural inspection; non-destructive testing (NDT) inspection; dimensional inspection; repair and replacement; reassembly; and testing and break in.

notes.front: What should be the first step for any engine to be completely overhauled?
notes.back: A runout check of its crankshaft or propeller shaft.
notes.explanation: A shaft beyond runout limits must be replaced, so the question is settled before other work.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “General Overhaul Procedures”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: Any engine to be overhauled completely should receive a runout check of its crankshaft or propeller shaft as a first step.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes an area of roughened scratches or marks, usually from foreign matter between moving parts or surfaces?
notes.back: Abrasion.
notes.explanation: Unlike scoring’s deep scratches, abrasion is a roughened patch of many marks left by grit carried between the surfaces.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Abrasion—an area of roughened scratches or marks usually caused by foreign matter between moving parts or surfaces.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes surface damage due to excessive heat?
notes.back: Burning.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives improper fit, defective lubrication or over-temperature operation as the usual sources of the heat.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Burning—surface damage due to excessive heat.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes polishing of one surface by sliding contact with a smooth, harder surface, usually with no metal removed?
notes.back: Burnishing.
notes.explanation: Unlike chafing or abrasion, it leaves the surface polished rather than worn; usually no metal is displaced or removed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Burnishing—polishing of one surface by sliding contact with a smooth, harder surface. Usually no displacement nor removal of metal.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a sharp or roughened projection of metal, usually from machine processing?
notes.back: Burr.
notes.explanation: It is metal left standing above the surface by machining, where most other defects cut into or wear the surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Burr—a sharp or roughened projection of metal usually resulting from machine processing.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes wear from a rubbing action between two parts under light pressure?
notes.back: Chafing.
notes.explanation: Light pressure is what keeps it mild; under high loads the rubbing can become galling, where metal transfers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Chafing—a condition caused by a rubbing action between two parts under light pressure that results in wear.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes breaking away of pieces of material, usually from excessive stress concentration or careless handling?
notes.back: Chipping.
notes.explanation: Flaking, by contrast, usually comes from defective plating or excessive loading rather than stress concentration.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Chipping—breaking away of pieces of material, that is usually caused by excessive stress concentration or careless handling.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes loss of metal by chemical or electrochemical action, with products easily removed mechanically?
notes.back: Corrosion.
notes.explanation: Iron rust is the handbook’s example: the loss is chemical, not the mechanical wear of abrasion or erosion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Corrosion—loss of metal by a chemical or electrochemical action. The corrosion products are easily removed by mechanical means.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a partial separation of material, usually from vibration, overloading, internal stresses, defective assembly or fatigue?
notes.back: Crack.
notes.explanation: Its depth may run from a few thousandths of an inch to the full thickness of the piece.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Crack—a partial separation of material usually caused by vibration, overloading, internal stresses, defective assembly, or fatigue.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes loss of metal to an appreciable depth over a long, narrow area by mechanical means?
notes.back: Cut.
notes.explanation: The handbook likens it to damage from a saw blade, chisel, or sharp-edged stone striking a glancing blow.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Cut—loss of metal, usually to an appreciable depth over a relatively long and narrow area, by mechanical means

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a small, rounded depression, usually from being struck with a rounded object?
notes.back: Dent.
notes.explanation: A sharp object would leave a V-bottomed nick instead; the rounded hollow points to a blunt, rounded blow.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Dent—a small, rounded depression in a surface usually caused by the part being struck with a rounded object.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes loss of metal from the surface by the mechanical action of foreign objects such as grit or fine sand?
notes.back: Erosion.
notes.explanation: The eroded area is rough and may show lines in the direction the foreign material moved across it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Erosion—loss of metal from the surface by mechanical action of foreign objects, such as grit or fine sand.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes small pieces of metal or coating breaking loose, usually from defective plating or excessive loading?
notes.back: Flaking.
notes.explanation: Chipping, by contrast, usually comes from stress concentration or careless handling rather than bad plating.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Flaking—the breaking loose of small pieces of metal or coated surfaces, that is usually caused by defective plating or excessive loading.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes surface erosion from minute movement between two parts clamped together under considerable unit pressure?
notes.back: Fretting.
notes.explanation: Once enough movement and load transfer metal between the clamped parts, the damage is called galling instead.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Fretting—a condition of surface erosion caused by minute movement between two parts usually clamped together with considerable unit pressure.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a furrowing in which metal is displaced with a torn effect, usually from material between close moving parts?
notes.back: Gouging.
notes.explanation: The torn edges set it apart from grooving, whose channel has rounded, smooth edges.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Gouging—a furrowing condition in which a displacement of metal has occurred (a torn effect). It is usually caused by a piece of metal, or foreign material, between close moving parts.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a recess or channel with rounded, smooth edges, usually from faulty alignment of parts?
notes.back: Grooving.
notes.explanation: Its smooth, rounded edges set it apart from the torn furrow of gouging.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Grooving—a recess, or channel, with rounded and smooth edges usually caused by faulty alignment of parts.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes foreign material entirely within a portion of metal, introduced during manufacture?
notes.back: Inclusion.
notes.explanation: Because it lies wholly inside the metal, it was put there by rolling or forging, not by wear in service.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Inclusion—presence of foreign or extraneous material entirely within a portion of metal. Such material is introduced during the manufacture of rod, bar, or tubing by rolling or forging.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a sharp-sided gouge or depression with a V-shaped bottom, usually from careless handling of tools and parts?
notes.back: Nick.
notes.explanation: The V-shaped bottom separates a nick from a dent, whose depression is small and rounded.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Nick—a sharp-sided gouge or depression with a V-shaped bottom, that is generally the result of careless handling of tools and parts.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a series of blunt depressions in a surface?
notes.back: Peening.
notes.explanation: A dent is a single small rounded depression; peening is a whole series of blunt ones.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Peening—a series of blunt depressions in a surface.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a build-up or rolling of metal from one area to another, usually from poor lubrication, clearances or foreign matter?
notes.back: Pick up, or scuffing.
notes.explanation: Scoring scratches metal away; pick up instead moves metal from one area and builds it up on another.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Pick up or scuffing—a buildup or rolling of metal from one area to another, that is usually caused by insufficient lubrication, clearances, or foreign matter.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes small, irregular hollows in the surface, usually from corrosion or minute mechanical chipping?
notes.back: Pitting.
notes.explanation: The handbook follows the list by saying that all gears should be examined for evidence of pitting or excessive wear.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Pitting—small hollows of irregular shape in the surface, usually caused by corrosion or minute mechanical chipping of surfaces.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes shallow, thin lines or marks from fine foreign particles during operation or contact during handling?
notes.back: Scratches.
notes.explanation: The same cause, foreign particles between moving parts, produces scoring when the scratches are deep.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Scratches—shallow, thin lines or marks, varying in degree of depth and width, caused by presence of fine foreign particles during operation or contact with other parts during handling.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a local change in colour giving a noticeably different appearance from the surrounding area?
notes.back: Stain.
notes.explanation: The definition names only a local colour change, with nothing said about metal being lost or moved.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Stain—a change in color, locally, causing a noticeably different appearance from the surrounding area.

notes.front: Which engine-part defect term describes a displacement of material beyond the normal contour, a local bulge or bump, usually with no metal loss?
notes.back: Upsetting.
notes.explanation: It bulges outward where a dent sinks inward, and usually means that no metal has been lost.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Upsetting—a displacement of material beyond the normal contour or surface (a local bulge or bump). Usually indicates no metal loss.

notes.front: What does any evidence of galling on a connecting rod require?
notes.back: Rejection of the complete rod assembly.
notes.explanation: Galling distorts the metal and weakens the rod’s structure much as corrosion does.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshaft & Connecting Rods”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: Evidence of any galling is sufficient reason for rejecting the complete rod assembly.

notes.front: What must never be used on a bearing or contact surface when removing hard carbon?
notes.back: Wire brushes or metal scrapers.
notes.explanation: Machined surfaces must not be damaged during brushing, scraping or grit-blasting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Removing Hard Carbon”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: In particular, wire brushes and metal scrapers must never be used on any bearing or contact surface.

notes.front: What does the manufacturer’s table of limits list?
notes.back: Serviceable limits and the new-part maximum and minimum dimensions.
notes.explanation: Measured parts and clearances are compared with it in the dimensional inspection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dimensional Inspection”, p. 10-7
notes.evidence: These specs are listed in a table of limits, which lists serviceable limits and the manufacturer’s new part maximum and minimum dimensions.

notes.front: What are two measurements taken in the dimensional inspection of a cylinder barrel?
notes.back: Any two: maximum taper; maximum out-of-roundness; bore diameter; step; fit between piston skirt and cylinder.
notes.explanation: Wear shows up as each of these, and each has a limit.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Barrel”, p. 10-7
notes.evidence: Dimensional inspection of the barrel consists of the following measurements: 1. Maximum taper of cylinder walls. 2. Maximum out-of-roundness.

notes.front: At how many positions must cylinder barrel diameters be measured?
notes.back: At least two positions 90° apart in the plane being measured.
notes.explanation: More than two may be needed to find the maximum wear.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Barrel”, p. 10-8
notes.evidence: All measurements involving cylinder barrel diameters must be taken at a minimum of two positions 90° apart in the particular plane being measured.

notes.front: How is crankshaft runout checked?
notes.back: With the shaft in V-blocks at the manual’s support points, using a surface plate and dial indicator.
notes.explanation: If the total indicator reading exceeds the table of limits, the shaft must not be reused.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshaft”, p. 10-9
notes.evidence: Place the crankshaft in V-blocks, supported at the locations specified in the applicable engine overhaul manual as in Figure 10-7. Using a surface plate and a dial indicator, measure the shaft runout.

notes.front: What is the maximum runout of a refaced valve seat?
notes.back: 0.002 inch, checked with a special dial indicator.
notes.explanation: The seat must be true to the valve guide.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Refacing Valve Seats”, p. 10-14
notes.evidence: Runout of the seat is checked with a special dial indicator and should not exceed 0.002 inch.

notes.front: Where should the Prussian blue contact band sit on the valve face?
notes.back: In the middle, one-third to two-thirds the width of the face.
notes.explanation: Contact too high or too low is corrected by narrowing the seat with a different-angle stone.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Refacing Valve Seats”, p. 10-14
notes.evidence: The contact surface should be one-third to two-thirds the width of the valve face and in the middle of the face.

notes.front: What interference angle may be ground on a valve face?
notes.back: 0.5° or 1.5° less than the standard angle, and only if the manufacturer approves it.
notes.explanation: The narrow line contact concentrates the seating load for a more positive seal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Reconditioning”, p. 10-14
notes.evidence: Usually, valves are ground to the standard angles of 30° or 45°. However, in some instances, an interference fit of 0.5° or 1.5° less than the standard angle may be ground on the valve face.

notes.front: How is a lapped valve tested for leaks?
notes.back: Hold the installed valve by its stem and pour kerosene or solvent into the port, watching for leakage into the chamber.
notes.explanation: If it leaks, lapping continues until the leakage stops.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Lapping & Leak Testing”, p. 10-17
notes.evidence: This is done by installing the valve in the cylinder, holding the valve by the stem with the fingers, and pouring kerosene or solvent into the valve port.

notes.front: What are the standard aircraft cylinder oversizes?
notes.back: 0.010, 0.015, 0.020 or 0.030 inch, where the manufacturer allows them.
notes.explanation: Thin walls and a nitrided surface limit how much can be ground away.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Grinding & Honing”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: Generally, standard aircraft cylinder oversizes are 0.010 inch, 0.015 inches, 0.020 inch, or 0.030 inch.

notes.front: What dual purpose does the engine run-in test serve?
notes.back: It runs in the piston rings and burnishes the bearings, and gives information to evaluate performance and condition.
notes.explanation: An engine’s reliability is in question until it has passed the cell test.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Testing Reciprocating Engines”, p. 10-20
notes.evidence: The test serves a dual purpose. First, it accomplishes piston ring run-in and bearing burnishing. Second, it provides valuable information that it used to evaluate engine performance and determine engine condition.

notes.front: Before removing the push rods, where should the piston be put, and why?
notes.back: At top dead centre on the compression stroke, which relieves pressure on both rocker arms.
notes.explanation: Both valves are closed at that point.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Removal”, p. 10-41
notes.evidence: Before removing the pushrods, turn the crankshaft until the piston is at top dead center on the compression stroke. This relieves the pressure on both intake and exhaust rocker arms.

notes.front: In removing a cylinder, which hold-down nuts or screws stay on until last?
notes.back: Two located 180° apart, removed while the cylinder is supported.
notes.explanation: Two technicians working together help prevent the cylinder being damaged or dropped.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Removal”, p. 10-42
notes.evidence: Remove all the screws or nuts except two located 180° apart.

notes.front: Which way should the number stamped on the bottom of the piston head face at installation?
notes.back: Toward the front of the engine.
notes.explanation: This ensures the piston faces in the right direction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Installation”, p. 10-42
notes.evidence: Be sure that the piston faces in the right direction. The piston number stamped on the bottom of the piston head should face toward the front of the engine.

notes.front: How are cylinder hold-down nuts torqued?
notes.back: With a slow, steady motion to the specified value, holding tension until the nut tightens no more.
notes.explanation: Up to a quarter turn more may come while the torque is held; the nuts are then safetied.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Installation”, p. 10-43
notes.evidence: Apply the torque with a slow, steady motion until the prescribed value is reached. Hold the tension on the wrench for a sufficient length of time to ensure that the nut or cap-screw tightens no more at the prescribed torque value.

notes.front: According to Advisory Circular 43.13-1B, why must cylinder hold-down nuts be tightened to the recommended torque?
notes.back: To prevent improper stressing and ensure even loading on the cylinder flange.
notes.explanation: The circular also discourages fitting baffles, brackets or clips under these nuts.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B, Change 1, chapter 8, paragraph 8-7, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: They must be tightened to the recommended torque limits to prevent improper stressing and to ensure even loading on the cylinder flange.

notes.front: In a cold cylinder check, what does a cold or only slightly warm cylinder indicate?
notes.back: Lack of combustion or incomplete combustion in that cylinder.
notes.explanation: The check is made with a cold cylinder indicator.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cold Cylinder Check”, p. 10-43
notes.evidence: The tendency for any cylinder, or cylinders, to be cold, or to be only slightly warm, indicates lack of combustion or incomplete combustion within the cylinder.

notes.front: What are the three types of engine storage?
notes.back: Active, temporary and indefinite.
notes.explanation: The extent of preservation depends on how long the engine will be inactive.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Corrosion-Preventive Materials”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: There are three types of engine storage: active engine, temporary, and indefinite.

notes.front: What defines an engine in active storage?
notes.back: At least one continuous hour of operation with oil at 165–200 °F, and storage not exceeding 30 days.
notes.explanation: Running the engine evaporates moisture and coats parts with oil.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Corrosion-Preventive Materials”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: An engine in active storage is defined as having at least one continuous hour of operation with an oil temperature of at least 165 °F to 200 °F and storage time not to exceed 30 days.

notes.front: How long is temporary storage, and when is storage indefinite?
notes.back: Temporary: not flown for 30 to 90 days; indefinite: not flown for over 90 days, or removed for an extended time.
notes.explanation: Longer inactivity calls for fuller preservation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Corrosion-Preventive Materials”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: Temporary storage describes an aircraft and engine that is not flown for 30 to 90 days, and indefinite storage is for an aircraft not to be flown for over 90 days or is removed from the aircraft for extended time.

notes.front: After the final corrosion-preventive spraying of the cylinders, why must the crankshaft not be moved?
notes.back: It would break the seal of mixture between pistons and cylinder walls and scrape the coating off.
notes.explanation: A sign on the engine warns against turning the crankshaft and gives the preservation date.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Preservation & Return to Service”, p. 8-19
notes.evidence: The crankshaft must not be moved after this final spraying, or the seal of corrosion-preventive mixture between the pistons and cylinder walls are broken.

notes.front: How is the type I concentrate of the light corrosion-preventive mixture blended?
notes.back: Three parts of the specified engine oil to one part of concentrate.
notes.explanation: Type II comes ready-mixed, and type III is ready-mixed for turbine engines only.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Corrosion-Preventive Compounds”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: Type I is a concentrate and must be blended with three parts of MIL-L-22851 or MIL-L-6082C (SAE J1966) grade 1100 oil to one part of concentrate.

notes.front: At what relative humidity does treated silica gel reach a natural or white colour?
notes.back: 60 percent.
notes.explanation: Some plug gel can be dried by heating, which returns it to its original blue.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dehydrating Agents”, p. 8-19
notes.evidence: fading through the various shades of pink [Figure 8-18], until at 60 percent relative humidity it is a natural or white color.

notes.front: Below what relative humidity does corrosion not normally take place?
notes.back: 30 percent.
notes.explanation: So bright blue dehydrator plugs show internal corrosion is held to a minimum.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dehydrating Agents”, p. 8-19
notes.evidence: When the relative humidity is less than 30 percent, corrosion does not normally take place.

notes.front: At what pressure is dehydrated air forced into a sealed metal engine container?
notes.back: About 5 psi.
notes.explanation: The pressure is rechecked occasionally, since temperature changes affect it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Shipping Containers”, p. 8-21
notes.evidence: dehydrated air at approximately 5 pounds per square inch (psi) pressure is forced into the container.

notes.front: How often are humidity indicators normally inspected on engines in wooden shipping cases and in metal containers?
notes.back: Wooden cases every 30 days; metal containers every 180 days under normal conditions.
notes.explanation: If the envelope must be opened to see the indicator, the wooden-case interval may extend to 90 days.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Inspection of Stored Engines”, p. 8-21
notes.evidence: Normally, the humidity indicators on engines stored in shipping cases are inspected every 30 days.

notes.front: During depreservation of a radial engine, why check the lower cylinders and intake pipes for compound?
notes.back: Excess compound settles there and could cause a hydraulic lock on starting.
notes.explanation: It can be drained through an open intake valve or removed with a hand pump.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Depreservation of an Engine”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: On radial engines, the inside of the lower cylinders and intake pipes should be carefully checked for the presence of excessive corrosion-preventive compound that has drained from throughout the interior of the engine and settled at these low points.

notes.front: May the holder of a powerplant certificate maintain and inspect light-sport engines?
notes.back: Yes, provided they meet all applicable regulations.
notes.explanation: A sport pilot may do only preventive maintenance, on an aircraft they own or operate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Personnel Authorized to Perform Inspection & Maintenance on Light-Sport Engines”, p. 11-2
notes.evidence: Given they meet all applicable regulations, the holder of a powerplant certificate can perform maintenance and inspections on light-sport engines.

notes.front: How long must the training course be for a light-sport repairman maintenance rating with airplane class privileges?
notes.back: At least 120 hours.
notes.explanation: An inspection rating needs a separate 16-hour course.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Personnel Authorized to Perform Inspection & Maintenance on Light-Sport Engines”, p. 11-2
notes.evidence: For airplane class privileges: 120 hours.

notes.front: Which of the Rotax 447 and 503 two-strokes has dual ignition?
notes.back: The 503; the 447 has a single ignition system.
notes.explanation: Both are breakerless, magneto capacitor discharge designs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Two-Cycle, Two Cylinder Rotax Engine”, p. 11-4
notes.evidence: The typical ignition system is a breakerless ignition system with a dual ignition system used on the 503, and a single ignition system used on the 447 engine series.

notes.front: In what ratio are the smaller Rotax two-cycle engines designed to run on premixed oil and gasoline?
notes.back: 1:50, which is 2 percent oil.
notes.explanation: Engines with oil injection instead feed pure gasoline to the carburettors.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Lubrication Systems”, p. 11-4
notes.evidence: Generally, the smaller two cycle engines are designed to run on a mixture of gasoline and 2 percent oil that is premixed in the fuel tank. The engines are planned to run on an oilgasoline mixture of 1:50.

notes.front: How is the Rotax 914 cooled?
notes.back: Liquid cooling of the cylinder heads and ram-air cooling of the cylinders.
notes.explanation: The heads’ coolant runs in a closed circuit with an expansion tank.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Rotax 912/914”, p. 11-6
notes.evidence: The cooling system of the Rotax 914, shown in Figure 11-7, is designed for liquid cooling of the cylinder heads and ram-air cooling of the cylinders.

notes.front: In pneumatic synchronisation of twin carburettors, how are they adjusted?
notes.back: To equal flow rate at idle, using a suitable flow meter or vacuum gauges, after mechanical synchronisation.
notes.explanation: If a correction of more than ½ turn is needed, mechanical synchronisation is repeated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pneumatic Synchronization”, p. 11-18
notes.evidence: Mechanical synchronization should have already been accomplished. The two carburetors are adjusted to equal flow rate at idling by use of a suitable flow meter or vacuum gauges (1).

notes.front: What counts as a sudden stoppage?
notes.back: Engine speed going to zero in less than one complete propeller revolution, from seizure or a blade striking an object.
notes.explanation: It can come from gear collapse, nosing over or a crash landing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Sudden Stoppage or Propeller Strike”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: Either can be caused by engine seizure or by one or more of the propeller blades striking an object in such a way that revolutions per minute (rpm) goes to zero in less than one complete revolution of the propeller.

notes.front: After a sudden reduction in speed, what does finding heavy metal particles in the oil mean?
notes.back: A definite engine failure: the engine must be removed.
notes.explanation: Fine filings instead call for further inspection to judge serviceability.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Sudden Reduction in Speed”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Heavy metal particles in the oil indicate a definite engine failure, and the engine must be removed.

notes.front: In the magneto safety check, what does failure of the engine to cut out when switched to off indicate?
notes.back: Faulty ground connections: the magnetos are not secured at shutdown and may fire if the propeller is turned.
notes.explanation: This is why the check is treated as a safety problem.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Warm-Up”, p. 10-26
notes.evidence: This indicates a safety problem; the magnetos are not secured at shut down and may fire if the propeller is turned.

notes.front: A restorer describes a 12-cylinder engine whose cylinders sit in two inline banks about 60° apart. Which type is it?
notes.back: C: V-type engine
notes.choices:
A) Radial engine
B) Horizontally opposed engine
C) V-type engine
D) Inline engine
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a radial arranges its cylinders round a central crankcase. B is wrong: opposed banks are directly opposite each other, 180° apart. D is wrong: an inline engine has a single bank.
notes.explanation: Two inline banks set about 60° apart is the V-type arrangement, and most V-types had 12 cylinders.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “V-Type Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: In V-type engines, the cylinders are arranged in two inline banks generally set 60° apart. Most of the engines have 12 cylinders

notes.front: A crop-spraying aeroplane’s engine has nine cylinders set around a central crankcase, all in one row. How is it classified?
notes.back: B: Single-row radial engine
notes.choices:
A) Double-row radial
B) Single-row radial engine
C) Inverted inline engine
D) V-type engine
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a double-row radial has two rows, one in front of the other. C is wrong: an inline engine’s cylinders run along the crankshaft, not round it. D is wrong: a V-type has two inline banks.
notes.explanation: Cylinders arranged radially about a central crankcase in one row make a single-row radial.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Radial Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: The radial engine consists of a row, or rows, of cylinders arranged radially about a central crankcase.

notes.front: A designer wants low-vibration engines with a narrow silhouette for the wings of a light twin. Which arrangement suits best?
notes.back: B: Horizontally opposed
notes.choices:
A) Radial
B) Horizontally opposed
C) V-type
D) Inverted inline
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a radial has a large frontal area. C is wrong: V-types are mostly limited to older aircraft. D is wrong: the air-cooled inline is confined to very old light aircraft.
notes.explanation: The handbook names the opposed engine’s narrow silhouette as ideal for wing installation on twins, along with its low weight-to-horsepower ratio.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Opposed or O-Type Engines”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: The opposed-type engine has a low weight-to-horsepower ratio, and its narrow silhouette makes it ideal for horizontal installation on the aircraft wings (twin engine applications).

notes.front: After intake pipe work on an un-supercharged radial, the engine idles faster than before but runs normally at open throttle. What is the likely cause?
notes.back: A: A slight leak at an intake pipe slip joint
notes.choices:
A) A slight leak at an intake pipe slip joint
B) Worn crankshaft main bearings
C) Late ignition timing
D) Rich mixture from a leaking primer
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong: a rich mixture would not raise idle speed this way. B is wrong: bearing wear does not lean the mixture. C is wrong: late timing shows as a slow drop in the magneto check, not a fast idle.
notes.explanation: Outside pressure exceeds inside pressure at idle, so a small leak draws in air and slightly leans the mixture.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankcase Section”, p. 1-6
notes.evidence: If the slip joint connection has a slight leakage, the engine may idle fast due to a slight leaning of the mixture.

notes.front: At overhaul, scoring is found on the crankshaft surface that runs in a main bearing and is the shaft’s centre of rotation. Which part is it?
notes.back: C: Main journal
notes.choices:
A) Crankpin
B) Crank cheek
C) Main journal
D) Flyweight
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the crankpin is off-centre and carries the connecting rod. B is wrong: the cheek joins crankpin to journal. D is wrong: flyweights are attached to the shaft but are not a true part of it.
notes.explanation: The journal is the part supported by, and rotating in, a main bearing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshafts”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: The journal is supported by, and rotates in, a main bearing. It serves as the center of rotation of the crankshaft.

notes.front: An engine vibrates at the frequency of its power impulses even though its crankshaft is statically balanced. Which device is designed to counter this?
notes.back: A: Dynamic dampers on the crankshaft
notes.choices:
A) Dynamic dampers on the crankshaft
B) A stiffer crankcase
C) A heavier propeller
D) Oversize main bearings
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: a heavy propeller adds gyroscopic loads rather than damping vibration. B is wrong: stiffness resists bending moments but does not cancel impulses. D is wrong: bearing size does not change impulse vibration.
notes.explanation: A damper’s pendulum frequency matches the power impulses and it swings out of time with the vibration.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dynamic Dampers”, p. 1-9
notes.evidence: When the vibration frequency of the crankshaft occurs, the pendulum oscillates out of time with the crankshaft vibration, thus reducing vibration to a minimum.

notes.front: Which connecting-rod type would you expect in a horizontally opposed engine?
notes.back: A: Plain-type rods
notes.choices:
A) Plain-type rods
B) Fork-and-blade rods
C) Master-and-articulated rods
D) A split-type master rod
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: fork-and-blade rods are used primarily in V-type engines. C is wrong: master-and-articulated rods are for radial engines. D is wrong: a split master rod belongs to a radial assembly.
notes.explanation: Plain-type rods, each with its own cap and two-piece bearing, are used in inline and opposed engines.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Plain-Type Connecting Rods”, p. 1-11
notes.evidence: Plain-type connecting rods are used in inline and opposed engines.

notes.front: A 14-cylinder, two-row radial is being overhauled. How many master rods and articulated rods should it have?
notes.back: D: Two master rods and 12 articulated rods
notes.choices:
A) One master rod and 13 articulated rods
B) Seven master rods and seven articulated rods
C) Two master rods and 14 articulated rods
D) Two master rods and 12 articulated rods
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: each row has its own master rod. B is wrong: there is only one master rod per row. C is wrong: the two pistons on master rods need no articulated rods.
notes.explanation: Each row has one master rod; every other piston in the row hangs on an articulated rod.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Master-and-Articulated Rod Assembly”, p. 1-9
notes.evidence: In a radial engine, the piston in one cylinder in each row is connected to the crankshaft by a master rod. All other pistons in the row are connected to the master rod by articulated rods.

notes.front: A cylinder wall shows scoring in line with the piston pin. What should the inspector suspect?
notes.back: B: A missing or worn soft plug in the pin end
notes.choices:
A) A cam ground piston
B) A missing or worn soft plug in the pin end
C) Too many compression rings
D) A tapered-face compression ring
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: cam grinding affects piston shape when cold, not the pin ends. C is wrong: ring count does not bring the pin into contact with the wall. D is wrong: a tapered face reduces friction.
notes.explanation: The pin must be held so its ends do not score the wall, and the soft aluminium plug provides the bearing surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Pin”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The piston pin must be held in place to prevent the pin ends from scoring the cylinder walls. A plug of relatively soft aluminum in the pin end provides a good bearing surface against the cylinder wall.

notes.front: A replacement cylinder has a chromium-plated barrel. Which rings should go with it?
notes.back: B: Cast iron rings
notes.choices:
A) Chrome-plated rings in every groove
B) Cast iron rings
C) Chrome-plated rings in the top groove only
D) Any rings of the correct size
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: chrome rings must never be used on chrome cylinders. C is wrong: even the top groove must not carry a chrome ring here. D is wrong: ring material matters, not just size.
notes.explanation: Chrome rings are for steel walls; chromium-plated cylinders take cast iron rings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Barrels”, p. 1-15
notes.evidence: Chromium-plated cylinders should use cast iron rings.

notes.front: An engine shows high oil consumption and thick carbon on the piston heads, plugs and valve heads. Which rings are most likely at fault?
notes.back: A: The oil control rings
notes.choices:
A) The oil control rings
B) The compression rings
C) The knuckle pin bushings
D) The valve springs
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: compression rings stop gas escaping, not oil entering. C is wrong: knuckle pins are rod parts. D is wrong: springs close the valves.
notes.explanation: The oil control rings regulate the oil film; too much oil in the chamber burns into thick carbon.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Oil Control Rings”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: If too much oil enters the combustion chamber, it burns and leaves a thick coating of carbon on the combustion chamber walls, the piston head, the spark plugs, and the valve heads.

notes.front: At the factory, how is an aluminium cylinder head joined gastight to its steel barrel?
notes.back: C: The heated head is screwed onto the chilled barrel
notes.choices:
A) It is welded to the barrel
B) It is bolted on with a copper gasket
C) The heated head is screwed onto the chilled barrel
D) The cold head is pressed onto a heated barrel
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: aluminium and steel are not welded here. B is wrong: no gasket is used in this joint. D is wrong: the temperatures are the other way round.
notes.explanation: As the head cools and contracts and the barrel warms and expands, the threaded joint becomes gastight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinders”, p. 1-14
notes.evidence: At assembly, the cylinder head is expanded by heating and then screwed down on the cylinder barrel, which has been chilled.

notes.front: Measuring a new cylinder, a technician finds the very top of the bore smaller than further down. What is the likely explanation?
notes.back: C: The cylinder has an intentional choke
notes.choices:
A) The barrel is bent
B) The cylinder has a ridge from ring wear
