C) The cylinder has an intentional choke
D) The bore is out-of-round
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a bend would show as flange or skirt damage, not a smaller top. B is wrong: a new cylinder has no wear ridge. D is wrong: out-of-roundness compares diameters 90° apart.
notes.explanation: Choke makes the top smaller to compensate for wear and expansion, which complicates taper measurement.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Barrel”, p. 10-8
notes.evidence: Cylinder choke is where the top of the cylinder has been made with the very top diameter of the cylinder smaller, to compensate for wear and expansion during operation.

notes.front: An opposed engine is mounted as a pusher, propeller facing aft. From where do you view it to name its right side?
notes.back: C: From the accessory end
notes.choices:
A) From the pilot’s seat
B) From the propeller end
C) From the accessory end
D) From the left wing tip
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the propeller end is the front, the wrong viewpoint. A is wrong: the pilot of a pusher faces forward, away from the engine, so the pilot’s right is the engine’s left. D is wrong: sides are named from the rear, not from a wing.
notes.explanation: Left and right are always named looking from the rear, or accessory, end, however the engine is mounted.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Numbering”, p. 1-15
notes.evidence: When referring to the right side or left side of an engine, always assume the view is from the rear or accessory end.

notes.front: On a nine-cylinder radial, which cylinder fires next after No. 9?
notes.back: D: No. 2
notes.choices:
A) No. 1
B) No. 3
C) No. 8
D) No. 2
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: No. 1 follows No. 8, at the end of the even cylinders. C is wrong: No. 8 is the last even cylinder. B is wrong: No. 3 follows No. 1.
notes.explanation: Odd cylinders fire in succession, then even ones, so after the last odd cylinder comes No. 2.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Single-Row Radial Engines”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: The firing order of a nine-cylinder radial engine is 1-3-5-7-9-2-4-6-8.

notes.front: On a 14-cylinder double-row radial, cylinder No. 10 has just fired. Which fires next?
notes.back: C: No. 5
notes.choices:
A) No. 19
B) No. 11
C) No. 5
D) No. 1
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: there is no cylinder 19; adding 9 goes above 14. B is wrong: adjacent numbers are in different rows but are not next in this order. D is wrong: that would be subtracting 9.
notes.explanation: Adding 9 to 10 exceeds 14, so subtract 5 instead.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Double-Row Radial Engines”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: start with any number from 1 to 14 and add 9 or subtract 5 (these are called the firing order numbers), whichever gives an answer between 1 and 14, inclusive.

notes.front: Two valves from one cylinder look alike, but one has a flat milled on its tip. What should the mechanic conclude?
notes.back: D: It is the intake valve, and they are not interchangeable
notes.choices:
A) It is the exhaust valve; they are interchangeable
B) It is a sodium-filled valve
C) The tip was damaged in service
D) It is the intake valve, and they are not interchangeable
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the flat marks the intake valve, and the faces differ in material. B is wrong: sodium filling is not marked by a flat. C is wrong: the flat is an identification mark.
notes.explanation: Similar intake and exhaust valves have faces of different material, and the flat identifies the intake.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Construction”, p. 1-18
notes.evidence: Although these valves are similar, they are not interchangeable since the faces of the valves are constructed of different material. The intake valve usually has a flat milled on the tip to identify it.

notes.front: A worn sodium-filled exhaust valve is to be scrapped. A trainee wants to cut it open to see inside. What is the right response?
notes.back: C: Forbid it: exposed sodium can cause fire or explosion
notes.choices:
A) Allow it if the valve is cold
B) Allow it under water
C) Forbid it: exposed sodium can cause fire or explosion
D) Allow it with eye protection
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: temperature does not make the sodium safe. B is wrong: the handbook allows no method of cutting it open. D is wrong: protection does not remove the fire or explosion risk.
notes.explanation: The handbook says a sodium-filled valve must under no circumstances be cut open.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Construction”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: Under no circumstances should a sodium-filled valve be cut open

notes.front: In an opposed engine’s valve train, which part converts the cam lobe’s rotation into reciprocating motion?
notes.back: D: The tappet assembly
notes.choices:
A) The rocker arm
B) The valve spring
C) The push rod
D) The tappet assembly
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the rocker arm passes the lift to the valve. C is wrong: the push rod only transmits the motion. B is wrong: the spring closes the valve.
notes.explanation: The tappet assembly follows the cam and passes reciprocating motion to the push rod.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Tappet Assembly”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: The function of the tappet assembly is to convert the rotational movement of the cam lobe into reciprocating motion and to transmit this motion to the push rod

notes.front: An opposed engine runs at 2,400 rpm. How fast does its camshaft turn?
notes.back: A: 1,200 rpm
notes.choices:
A) 1,200 rpm
B) 2,400 rpm
C) 4,800 rpm
D) 600 rpm
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: that doubles instead of halving. B is wrong: the camshaft is geared down. D is wrong: that is one quarter.
notes.explanation: The camshaft always turns at half crankshaft speed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Camshaft”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: The camshaft always rotates at one-half the crankshaft speed.

notes.front: At overhaul, a hydraulic-lifter engine assembled dry shows valve clearance outside the limits. How is it usually corrected?
notes.back: A: By fitting push rods of a different length
notes.choices:
A) By fitting push rods of a different length
B) By turning an adjusting screw and lock nut
C) By grinding the cam lobe
D) By oiling the lifter and rechecking
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that is how solid lifters are adjusted. C is wrong: cam lobes are not ground to set clearance. D is wrong: clearance is checked dry.
notes.explanation: Hydraulic lifters are adjusted at overhaul, usually with push rods of different lengths.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hydraulic Valve Tappets/Lifters”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: They are assembled dry (no lubrication), clearances checked, and adjustments are usually made by using push rods of different lengths.

notes.front: Why does each valve carry two or three springs, one inside the other?
notes.back: D: Each surges at a different speed, so surge is damped
notes.choices:
A) To double the valve lift
B) To let the valve open earlier
C) To keep the valve cooler
D) Each surges at a different speed, so surge is damped
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: lift is set by the cam lobe. B is wrong: timing is set by the cam. C is wrong: springs are not a cooling device.
notes.explanation: A single spring would surge at certain speeds; several springs vibrate at different speeds and damp each other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Valve Springs”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Each spring vibrates at a different engine speed and rapid damping out of all spring-surge vibrations during engine operation results.

notes.front: Which bearing type serves as the crankshaft main bearings of a high-power reciprocating engine?
notes.back: A: Straight roller bearings
notes.choices:
A) Straight roller bearings
B) Deep-groove ball bearings
C) Porous bushings
D) Tapered roller bearings
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: deep-groove ball bearings carry propeller thrust in radial nose sections. C is wrong: porous bushings serve small accessory shafts. D is wrong: tapered rollers are for combined radial and thrust loads.
notes.explanation: Straight roller bearings suit radial-only loads and are used for these main bearings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Roller Bearings”, p. 1-22
notes.evidence: Straight roller bearings are used in high power reciprocating aircraft engines for the crankshaft main bearings.

notes.front: A reduction gear has a sun gear on the crankshaft, a stationary bell gear, and pinions on a carrier fixed to the propeller shaft. How does the propeller turn?
notes.back: A: Same direction as the crankshaft, slower
notes.choices:
A) Same direction as the crankshaft, slower
B) Opposite direction, slower
C) Same direction, faster
D) Same direction and speed
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: opposite rotation comes when the cage is held and the bell gear drives the shaft. C is wrong: reduction gearing slows the propeller. D is wrong: the gears would then be pointless.
notes.explanation: The pinions walk round the fixed bell gear, carrying the carrier and propeller shaft round in the crankshaft’s direction at reduced speed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Propeller Reduction Gearing”, p. 1-23
notes.evidence: the ring in which they are mounted rotates the propeller shaft in the same direction as the crankshaft but at a reduced speed.

notes.front: A modern flat-six engine’s propeller shaft ends in a disc drilled for the propeller mounting bolts. Which type is it?
notes.back: B: Flanged
notes.choices:
A) Tapered
B) Flanged
C) Keyed
D) Splined
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a tapered shaft uses a keyway and retaining nut. D is wrong: splined shafts are generally on high-output radials. C is wrong: keying belongs to tapered shafts.
notes.explanation: A flanged shaft is drilled to accept the propeller mounting bolts and is used on most modern reciprocating engines.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Propeller Shafts”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Flanged propeller shafts are used on most modern reciprocating and turboprop engines. One end of the shaft is flanged with drilled holes to accept the propeller mounting bolts.

notes.front: Both valves are closed and the piston is rising; near the top, the spark fires. Which stroke is this?
notes.back: A: Compression
notes.choices:
A) Compression
B) Intake
C) Power
D) Exhaust
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: on intake the piston moves down with the intake valve open. C is wrong: on power the piston is driven down. D is wrong: on exhaust the exhaust valve is open.
notes.explanation: The rising piston compresses the charge after the intake valve closes, and the spark fires as it nears TDC.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Stroke”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: After the intake valve is closed, the continued upward travel of the piston compresses the air-fuel mixture to obtain the desired burning and expansion characteristics.

notes.front: The piston is rising from bottom dead centre with the exhaust valve open. Which stroke is this?
notes.back: A: Exhaust
notes.choices:
A) Exhaust
B) Power
C) Compression
D) Intake
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: on compression both valves are closed. B is wrong: on power the piston moves down. D is wrong: on intake the piston moves down.
notes.explanation: After the power stroke the rising piston pushes the burned gases out through the exhaust port.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Exhaust Stroke”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: As the piston travels through BDC at the completion of the power stroke and starts upward on the exhaust stroke, it begins to push the burned exhaust gases out the exhaust port.

notes.front: An engine’s intake valve opens 20° before top dead centre and its exhaust valve closes 15° after. How long is the valve overlap?
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the lead and lag add, they do not subtract. C is wrong: that is the lead alone. D is wrong: that is the lag alone.
notes.explanation: Overlap runs from the intake opening before TDC (valve lead) to the exhaust closing after it (valve lag).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Intake Stroke”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: the intake valve opens before TDC on the exhaust stroke (valve lead), and the closing of the exhaust valve is delayed considerably after the piston has passed TDC and has started the intake stroke (valve lag). This timing is called valve overlap

notes.front: A light-sport engine completes its whole operating cycle in one crankshaft revolution, with intake and exhaust in the same stroke. Which cycle is it?
notes.back: D: Two-stroke
notes.choices:
A) Four-stroke
B) Otto
C) Diesel four-stroke
D) Two-stroke
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a four-stroke needs two revolutions. C is wrong: a four-stroke diesel also needs two revolutions. B is wrong: the Otto cycle is the four-stroke cycle.
notes.explanation: One upstroke and one downstroke complete the two-stroke cycle in a single revolution.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Two-Stroke Cycle”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: Thus, the engine completes the operating cycle in one revolution of the crankshaft. The intake and exhaust functions are accomplished during the same stroke.

notes.front: An aircraft engine has no spark plugs and burns Jet A; fuel is sprayed in at maximum compression. Which cycle does it use?
notes.back: C: Diesel
notes.choices:
A) Rotary
B) Otto
C) Diesel
D) Two-stroke spark ignition
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the rotary cycle uses a three-sided rotor. B is wrong: the Otto cycle ignites with a spark. D is wrong: spark ignition needs spark plugs.
notes.explanation: The diesel cycle relies on high compression pressure and temperature to ignite fuel, and Jet A engines use a version of it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Diesel Cycle”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: Water and air cooled engines that can operate on JET A fuel (kerosene) use a version of the diesel cycle.

notes.front: A four-cylinder engine has a bore area of 20 square inches and a 4-inch stroke. What is its total piston displacement?
notes.back: C: 320 cubic inches
notes.choices:
A) 80 cubic inches
B) 100 cubic inches
C) 320 cubic inches
D) 160 cubic inches
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: that is one cylinder only. B is wrong: 100 adds the bore area to one cylinder’s volume (80 + 20) instead of multiplying by four cylinders. D is wrong: that uses two cylinders.
notes.explanation: Area × stroke gives 80 cubic inches per cylinder, multiplied by four cylinders.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Displacement”, p. 1-28
notes.evidence: For multicylinder engines, this product is multiplied by the number of cylinders to get the total piston displacement of the engine.

notes.front: A cylinder holds 150 cubic inches with the piston at the bottom of the stroke and 25 cubic inches with it at the top. What is the compression ratio?
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that uses the swept volume, 125, over 25. C is wrong: 7:1 counts the top volume twice, (150 + 25) ÷ 25. D is wrong: that is the swept volume, not a ratio.
notes.explanation: The ratio compares the volume at the bottom of the stroke with the volume at the top: 150 ÷ 25.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Ratio”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: The compression ratio of an engine is a comparison of the volume of space in a cylinder when the piston is at the bottom of the stroke to the volume of space when the piston is at the top of the stroke.

notes.front: A four-cylinder, four-stroke engine at 2,400 rpm has an indicated mean effective pressure of 100 psi, a 0.5 ft stroke and a 20 sq in piston area. What is its IHP?
notes.back: A: About 145 hp
notes.choices:
A) About 145 hp
B) About 291 hp
C) About 73 hp
D) About 36 hp
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that uses 2,400 rather than 1,200 power strokes a minute. C is wrong: that uses two cylinders. D is wrong: that uses one cylinder.
notes.explanation: N is half the rpm, 1,200; 100 × 0.5 × 20 × 1,200 × 4 is 4,800,000 ft-lb per minute, divided by 33,000.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Indicated Horsepower”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: rpm N = Number of power strokes per minute: 2 K = Number of cylinders

notes.front: On a test stand, a shaft delivers 300 lb-ft of torque at 2,500 rpm. About what BHP is that?
notes.back: A: About 143 hp
notes.choices:
A) About 143 hp
B) About 71 hp
C) About 23 hp
D) About 286 hp
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: that leaves out the 2π factor. B is wrong: that uses π instead of 2π. D is wrong: that doubles the result.
notes.explanation: 2π × 300 × 2,500 is about 4,712,000 ft-lb per minute; divided by 33,000 that is about 143 hp.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Brake Horsepower”, p. 1-32
notes.evidence: If work per revolution is multiplied by the rpm, the result is work per minute, or power. If the work is expressed in ft-lb per minute, this quantity is divided by 33,000.

notes.front: An engine develops 200 IHP and delivers 175 BHP. What are its friction horsepower and mechanical efficiency?
notes.back: D: 25 hp and 87.5%
notes.choices:
A) 175 hp and 87.5%
B) 25 hp and 114%
C) 25 hp and 12.5%
D) 25 hp and 87.5%
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: 175 is the BHP, not the friction loss. B is wrong: that divides IHP by BHP, the wrong way round. C is wrong: 12.5% is the share lost to friction.
notes.explanation: Friction horsepower is IHP minus BHP, and mechanical efficiency is BHP divided by IHP.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Mechanical Efficiency”, p. 1-35
notes.evidence: Brake horsepower is the useful power delivered to the propeller shaft. Indicated horsepower is the total hp developed in the cylinders. The difference between the two is friction horsepower (fhp), the power lost in overcoming friction.

notes.front: An engine delivers 1,200 BHP to a propeller that is 80 percent efficient. What is the THP?
notes.back: A: 960 hp
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: THP equals BHP only with a 100 percent efficient propeller. C is wrong: that divides by the efficiency. D is wrong: 240 hp is the power lost.
notes.explanation: THP is BHP multiplied by propeller efficiency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Thrust Horsepower”, p. 1-33
notes.evidence: For example, if an engine develops 1,000 bhp, and it is used with a propeller having 85 percent efficiency, the thrust horsepower of that engine-propeller combination is 85 percent of 1,000 or 850 thrust hp.

notes.front: An unsupercharged engine of 200 cubic inches displacement draws in 180 cubic inches of charge, corrected to standard conditions, per cycle. What is its volumetric efficiency?
notes.back: A: 90 percent
notes.choices:
A) 90 percent
B) 111 percent
C) 20 percent
D) 10 percent
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that divides the wrong way round. C is wrong: 20 is the shortfall in cubic inches, not a percentage. D is wrong: that is the shortfall as a percentage.
notes.explanation: Volumetric efficiency compares the corrected charge with the piston displacement: 180 ÷ 200.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Volumetric Efficiency”, p. 1-35
notes.evidence: It is a comparison of the volume of air-fuel charge (corrected for temperature and pressure) inducted into the cylinders to the total piston displacement of the engine.

notes.front: A piston engine burns 60 lb of fuel per hour while delivering 150 BHP. What is its SFC?
notes.back: C: 0.4 lb per hp per hour
notes.choices:
A) 2.5 lb per hp per hour
B) 0.25 lb per hp per hour
C) 0.4 lb per hp per hour
D) 9,000 lb per hp per hour
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: that divides BHP by fuel flow. B is wrong: 0.25 would mean only 37.5 lb of fuel an hour at 150 BHP. D is wrong: that multiplies instead of dividing.
notes.explanation: For a reciprocating engine SFC is fuel flow in pounds per hour divided by BHP.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Fuel Economy”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: for reciprocating engines the fuel flow (lb/hr) divided by brake horsepower.

notes.front: At overhaul, an engine that ran normally shows dished piston heads and broken ring lands. What does this indicate?
notes.back: D: Severe detonation in service
notes.choices:
A) Pre-oiling was skipped
B) Afterfiring
C) Hydraulic lock
D) Severe detonation in service
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: missed pre-oiling would affect bearings, not piston heads. B is wrong: afterfiring happens in the exhaust system. C is wrong: a hydraulic lock bends or breaks rods.
notes.explanation: Light detonation gives no flight deck warning, and its marks are often first found at teardown.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Detonation”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: When the engine is overhauled, however, the presence of severe detonation during its operation is indicated by dished piston heads, collapsed valve heads, broken ring lands

notes.front: In a high-power climb, the engine roughens, backfires and cylinder head temperature jumps suddenly. What should be done first?
notes.back: A: Retard the throttle
notes.choices:
A) Retard the throttle
B) Lean the mixture
C) Switch to one magneto
D) Increase manifold pressure
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: enriching, not leaning, lowers combustion temperature. C is wrong: the hot spot, not the ignition, is firing the charge. D is wrong: manifold pressure should be reduced.
notes.explanation: These are the signs of pre-ignition, and retarding the throttle cuts the fuel charge and heat.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pre-Ignition”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: The most obvious method of correcting pre-ignition is to reduce the cylinder temperature. The immediate step is to retard the throttle.

notes.front: An engine pops back through the induction system at idle but runs well at cruise and takeoff power. What is the most likely cause?
notes.back: D: An excessively lean idle mixture
notes.choices:
A) A cracked magneto
B) Worn piston rings
C) A rich cruise mixture
D) An excessively lean idle mixture
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a basic magneto failure would stop the engine or cut out at high speeds. C is wrong: a rich mixture causes afterfiring. B is wrong: rings do not cause idle-only backfiring.
notes.explanation: Backfiring confined to the idle range most likely comes from an excessively lean idle mixture.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Backfiring”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: In some instances, an engine backfires in the idle range but operates satisfactorily at medium and high power settings. The most likely cause, in this case, is an excessively lean idle mixture.

notes.front: Explosions occur in the exhaust, but the carburettor setting checks correct. What should be suspected, and how is it found?
notes.back: C: A dead or intermittent cylinder; the cold cylinder check
notes.choices:
A) A lean idle mixture; a compression test
B) Detonation; a borescope
C) A dead or intermittent cylinder; the cold cylinder check
D) A sticking tachometer; tapping the gauge
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a lean mixture causes backfiring in the induction system. B is wrong: detonation occurs inside the cylinder. D is wrong: a tachometer cannot cause exhaust explosions.
notes.explanation: Unburned mixture from a dead cylinder ignites in the exhaust, and the cold cylinder check finds such cylinders.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Afterfiring”, p. 10-31
notes.evidence: The unburned mixture from these dead cylinders passes into the exhaust system, where it ignites and burns.

notes.front: One cylinder’s valve clearance is set well below specification. How will that cylinder run at idle?
notes.back: C: Lean, because overlap lengthens
notes.choices:
A) Rich, because overlap shortens
B) No change, because the carburettor compensates
C) Lean, because overlap lengthens
D) Rich, because the exhaust stays shut
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: too little clearance lengthens overlap. B is wrong: the carburettor gives every cylinder the same mixture. D is wrong: less clearance opens valves longer, not shorter.
notes.explanation: A longer overlap draws more air or exhaust back into the cylinder at idle, leaning the mixture there.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Operational Effect of Valve Clearance”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: When valve clearance is less than it should be, the valve overlap period is lengthened. A greater than normal amount of air, or exhaust gases, is drawn back into the cylinder at idling speeds. As a result, the idle mixture is leaned out at the cylinder.

notes.front: A radial engine has stood for two hours. Pulling the propeller through, you meet a solid stop near top centre on a lower cylinder. What do you do?
notes.back: A: Remove a lower cylinder spark plug and turn in the direction of rotation
notes.choices:
A) Remove a lower cylinder spark plug and turn in the direction of rotation
B) Crank the engine with the starter to push through
C) Pull the propeller backwards to clear the liquid
D) Prime the engine and start it
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: forcing it risks a bent rod or blown cylinder. C is wrong: reverse rotation pushes liquid into the intake pipe. D is wrong: starting with a lock can wreck the engine.
notes.explanation: Liquid in the lower cylinder is incompressible; with a plug out, the piston expels it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Hydraulic Lock”, p. 10-25
notes.evidence: To eliminate a lock, remove either the front or rear spark plug of the lower cylinders and pull the propeller through in the direction of rotation.

notes.front: In the magneto check, the rpm falls slowly on the left magneto and quickly settles. What is the likely cause?
notes.back: C: Incorrect ignition timing or valve adjustment
notes.choices:
A) A cracked spark plug insulator
B) A broken ignition lead
C) Incorrect ignition timing or valve adjustment
D) A dead spark plug
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: faulty plugs take effect at once, a fast drop. B is wrong: faulty leads give a fast drop. D is wrong: a dead plug gives an instantaneous drop.
notes.explanation: Late timing lowers peak pressure gradually, so its power loss appears as a slow drop.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ground Check”, p. 10-27
notes.evidence: Slow rpm drop usually is caused by incorrect ignition timing or faulty valve adjustment.

notes.front: With the propeller at full low pitch, an engine now needs 31 inches of manifold pressure for an rpm that took 29 inches last month, same field and weather. What is likely?
notes.back: C: A dead cylinder or late ignition timing
notes.choices:
A) Early ignition timing
B) A strong head wind
C) A dead cylinder or late ignition timing
D) Normal variation
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: early timing gives low manifold pressure. B is wrong: a head wind raises rpm for a given pressure. D is wrong: identical conditions should agree within 1 inch.
notes.explanation: More power input for the same output means something is wrong, most often a dead cylinder or late timing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Power Check”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: A higher than normal manifold pressure usually indicates a dead cylinder or late ignition timing.

notes.front: Moving the mixture to idle cut-off, the rpm rises about 45 rpm before the engine dies. The manufacturer recommends about 20. What does this mean?
notes.back: B: The idle mixture is too rich
notes.choices:
A) The idle mixture is too lean
B) The idle mixture is too rich
C) The ignition timing is early
D) The idle mixture is correct
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: too lean shows as no rise or an immediate drop. D is wrong: a proper mixture rises less than the recommended figure. C is wrong: this check tests mixture, not timing.
notes.explanation: A rise greater than the recommended figure indicates the mixture is too rich, which fouls plugs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Power Check”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: An increase in rpm, but less than that recommended by the manufacturer (usually 20 rpm), indicates proper mixture strength. A greater increase indicates that the mixture is too rich.

notes.front: Which order stops an engine with an idle cut-off mixture control?
notes.back: B: Idle at 800–1,000 rpm, mixture to idle cut-off, ignition off when the propeller stops
notes.choices:
A) Ignition off, then mixture to idle cut-off
B) Idle at 800–1,000 rpm, mixture to idle cut-off, ignition off when the propeller stops
C) Throttle closed, ignition off, then mixture lean
D) Mixture to idle cut-off at takeoff power, then ignition off
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: switching off first leaves combustible charge in the cylinders. C is wrong: the mixture control, not the ignition, stops the engine. D is wrong: the engine is idled first.
notes.explanation: The ignition is switched off only after the propeller has stopped turning.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Stopping”, p. 10-29
notes.evidence: 2. Move the mixture control to the idle cutoff position. In a float-type carburetor, it equalizes the pressure in the float chamber and at the discharge nozzle. 3. After the propeller has stopped rotating, place the ignition switch in the off position.

notes.front: Using the chart, an opposed engine runs unevenly with low power, sluggish response, a red exhaust flame and black smoke. What remedy does the chart give?
notes.back: C: Check the primer and re-adjust the carburettor mixture
notes.choices:
A) Check fuel lines for dirt and check the fuel supply
B) Overhaul the engine
C) Check the primer and re-adjust the carburettor mixture
D) Install new piston rings
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: that is the chart’s remedy for a mixture too lean. B is wrong: nothing points to worn internals. D is wrong: rings are the remedy for oil consumption.
notes.explanation: Those symptoms are the chart’s signs of a mixture too rich.

image.alt: Table of six rows with columns Trouble, Probable cause and Remedy. Engine fails to start: overpriming, open throttle and unload engine by rotating the propeller. Engine fails to start: defective spark plugs, clean and re-gap or replace. Engine fails to idle properly: incorrect idle mixture, adjust mixture. Low power and engine running uneven: mixture too rich, shown by sluggish operation, red exhaust flame and black smoke, check primer and re-adjust carburettor mixture. Low power and engine running uneven: mixture too lean, shown by overheating or backfiring, check fuel lines for dirt or restrictions and check fuel supply. Low power and engine running uneven: incorrect valve clearance, adjust valve clearance.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), Figure 10-52

notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Troubleshooting”, p. 10-36
notes.evidence: Mixture too rich; indicated by sluggish engine • Check primer. Re-adjust carburetor mixture.

notes.front: A shop replaces pistons and rings, reconditions the cylinder walls and valve guides, and never splits the crankcase. What has it done?
notes.back: A: A top overhaul
notes.choices:
A) A top overhaul
B) A receiving inspection
C) A major overhaul
D) A major repair
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: a major overhaul disassembles the crankcase. B is wrong: receiving inspection only assesses the engine as received. D is wrong: the handbook calls it an engine repair procedure, not a major repair.
notes.explanation: Reconditioning the parts on top of the crankcase without complete dismantling is a top overhaul.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Top Overhaul”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: This means an overhaul of those parts on top of the crankcase, without completely dismantling the engine.

notes.front: A powerplant mechanic finishes a major overhaul, crankcase split, of an engine with an integral supercharger. Who may approve the engine for return to service?
notes.back: C: A holder of an inspection authorisation, if approved data were used
notes.choices:
A) The powerplant mechanic who did the work
B) Any certificated mechanic who inspects it
C) A holder of an inspection authorisation, if approved data were used
D) The aircraft owner
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: Section 65.87 of the regulations lets a powerplant mechanic approve only work that excludes major repairs. B is wrong: the same limit binds every mechanic, whoever inspects the work. D is wrong: an owner has no authority to approve maintenance for return to service.
notes.explanation: Splitting the crankcase of an engine with an integral supercharger is a powerplant major repair, and approving major repairs is an inspection authorisation privilege.
notes.source: 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition), PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration

notes.front: A bearing race removed with a hammer shows rounded dents matching the balls. Which defect term applies?
notes.back: B: Brinelling
notes.choices:
A) Galling
B) Brinelling
C) Pitting
D) Scoring
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: galling transfers metal between parts. C is wrong: pitting is irregular hollows, usually from corrosion. D is wrong: scoring is deep scratches.
notes.explanation: Rounded indentations on races from force during installation or removal are brinelling.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Brinelling—one or more indentations on bearing races, usually caused by high static loads or application of force during installation or removal.

notes.front: Two tightly clamped parts show surface erosion from tiny movements, with no metal carried from one to the other. Which term fits?
notes.back: B: Fretting
notes.choices:
A) Galling
B) Fretting
C) Burnishing
D) Upsetting
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: galling is fretting severe enough to transfer metal. C is wrong: burnishing is polishing by a harder surface. D is wrong: upsetting is a bulge with no metal loss.
notes.explanation: Fretting is erosion from minute movement between clamped parts; galling adds metal transfer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Fretting—a condition of surface erosion caused by minute movement between two parts usually clamped together with considerable unit pressure.

notes.front: A cylinder measures 4.018 inches at the top of the ring travel and 4.010 inches at the bottom. What is its taper?
notes.back: C: 0.008 inch
notes.choices:
A) 0.018 inch
B) 0.010 inch
C) 0.008 inch
D) 8.028 inches
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: that is part of the top diameter. B is wrong: that is part of the bottom diameter. D is wrong: taper is a difference, not a sum.
notes.explanation: Taper is the difference between top and bottom diameters, then compared with the table of limits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Barrel”, p. 10-8
notes.evidence: Taper of the cylinder walls is the difference between the diameter of the cylinder barrel at the bottom and the diameter at the top.

notes.front: A crankshaft’s runout slightly exceeds the table of limits. A colleague proposes straightening it in a press. What is correct?
notes.back: B: Reject it: it must not be reused or straightened
notes.choices:
A) Straighten it and re-nitride
B) Reject it: it must not be reused or straightened
C) Straighten it if the runout is under double the limit
D) Reuse it and recheck at the next overhaul
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: straightening ruptures the nitrided journal surfaces. C is wrong: the handbook allows no straightening. D is wrong: beyond limits it must not be reused.
notes.explanation: Straightening ruptures the nitrided journals and leads to eventual crankshaft failure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshaft”, p. 10-9
notes.evidence: If the total indicator reading exceeds the dimensions given in the manufacturer’s table of limits, the shaft must not be re-used. A bent crankshaft should not be straightened.

notes.front: Removing a cylinder, you find one of its cap-screws broken; the others look fine. What do you do?
notes.back: A: Discard all the cap-screws for that cylinder
notes.choices:
A) Discard all the cap-screws for that cylinder
B) Replace only the broken screw
C) Replace the broken screw and its neighbours
D) Re-torque the remaining screws
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the others may be seriously weakened. C is wrong: the rule covers every screw of that cylinder. D is wrong: weakened screws cannot be trusted at any torque.
notes.explanation: The remaining cap-screws may have been seriously weakened.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Removal”, p. 10-42
notes.evidence: If one cap-screw is found loose or broken at the time of cylinder removal, all the cap-screws for the cylinder should be discarded

notes.front: Fitting a cylinder over the piston, a technician rocks it; now the piston will not enter the bore. What most likely happened?
notes.back: C: A ring escaped the compressor and expanded
notes.choices:
A) The piston pin moved
B) The oil-seal ring doubled up
C) A ring escaped the compressor and expanded
D) The hold-down studs stretched
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the pin does not stop the piston entering. B is wrong: the seal ring is at the flange, not the bore. D is wrong: the studs are not loaded yet.
notes.explanation: Rocking can release a ring from the compressor before it enters the bore, and the expanded ring blocks the piston.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Cylinder Installation”, p. 10-42
notes.evidence: A ring released in this manner expands and prevents the piston from entering the cylinder.

notes.front: An aircraft will not fly for about 60 days. Which type of engine storage applies?
notes.back: C: Temporary
notes.choices:
A) Active
B) Indefinite
C) Temporary
D) Overhaul
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: active storage does not exceed 30 days. B is wrong: indefinite storage is over 90 days. D is wrong: there is no overhaul storage type.
notes.explanation: Temporary storage covers 30 to 90 days without flying.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Corrosion-Preventive Materials”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: Temporary storage describes an aircraft and engine that is not flown for 30 to 90 days

notes.front: The dehydrator plugs on a stored engine have turned from bright blue to lavender and pink. What does this show?
notes.back: C: Relative humidity has reached 30 percent or more, where corrosion can begin
notes.choices:
A) The corrosion-preventive mixture has drained
B) The silica gel is fresh
C) Relative humidity has reached 30 percent or more, where corrosion can begin
D) Humidity is below 30 percent
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: fresh, dry gel is bright blue. A is wrong: plug colour shows humidity, not the mixture level. D is wrong: lavender marks 30 percent and pink is higher.
notes.explanation: Corrosion does not normally occur below 30 percent relative humidity, where the gel is still blue.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dehydrating Agents”, p. 8-19
notes.evidence: becoming lavender at 30 percent relative humidity and fading through the various shades of pink

notes.front: A landing gear collapses on touchdown and the propeller stops within half a turn. What does the engine usually require?
notes.back: A: Replacement, or disassembly and inspection per the manufacturer
notes.choices:
A) Replacement, or disassembly and inspection per the manufacturer
B) A ground run and oil screen check only
C) A propeller track check only
D) Nothing if it restarts
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that approach suits a sudden reduction in speed, not a sudden stoppage. C is wrong: tracking does not reveal internal damage. D is wrong: hidden internal damage is likely.
notes.explanation: Speed going to zero in less than one revolution is a sudden stoppage, which can crack gear teeth or detune flyweights.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Sudden Stoppage or Propeller Strike”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: When sudden stoppage occurs, the engine usually requires replacement or disassembly and inspection as per manufacturer’s instructions.

notes.front: Before hand-turning the propeller of a preserved engine, which check protects against it firing?
notes.back: A: Magneto switches off and P-leads grounded
notes.choices:
A) Magneto switches off and P-leads grounded
B) Throttle wide open
C) Mixture set rich
D) Fuel selector on
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: the mixture should be at idle cut-off. B is wrong: the throttle should be closed. D is wrong: fuel on adds risk.
notes.explanation: An ungrounded magneto may fire when the propeller is turned.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Preservation & Return to Service”, p. 8-20
notes.evidence: Verify that magneto switches are connected to magnetos and that they are in the off position and P-leads are grounded.

notes.front: During a start, flames appear at the air intake. What should the operator do first?
notes.back: C: Continue cranking to start the engine and blow the fire out
notes.choices:
A) Stop cranking at once
B) Open the cowling to reach the fire
C) Continue cranking to start the engine and blow the fire out
D) Switch the magnetos off and wait
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the start is abandoned only if the engine will not start and the fire continues. B is wrong: the fireguard directs the agent into the intake. D is wrong: this leaves the fire burning.
notes.explanation: If the engine starts, it draws the fire through and blows it out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Extinguishing Engine Fires”, p. 3-5
notes.evidence: If an engine fire develops during the starting procedure, continue cranking to start the engine and blow out the fire.

notes.front: How does detonation differ from pre-ignition in when the charge ignites?
notes.back: Detonation: unburned charge ahead of the flame fronts explodes after ignition. Pre-ignition: burning starts before the timed spark.
notes.explanation: The two are linked: detonation often leads to pre-ignition.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Pre-Ignition”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: Pre-ignition, as the name implies, means that combustion takes place within the cylinder before the timed spark jumps across the spark plug terminals.

notes.front: How do backfiring and afterfiring differ in mixture and location?
notes.back: Backfiring: lean mixture, explosion in the induction system. Afterfiring: rich mixture, explosion in the exhaust system.
notes.explanation: For both, the correction is proper adjustment of the air-fuel mixture.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Afterfiring”, p. 10-31
notes.evidence: This causes an explosion in the exhaust system. Afterfiring is perhaps more common where long exhaust ducting retains greater amounts of unburned charges. As in the case of backfiring, the correction for afterfiring is the proper adjustment of the air-fuel mixture.

notes.front: How does static balance of a crankshaft differ from dynamic balance?
notes.back: Static: its weight is balanced about the axis. Dynamic: rotation and power-impulse forces balance so little vibration results.
notes.explanation: Dynamic dampers are fitted to bring vibration in operation to a minimum.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Crankshaft Balance”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: Crankshafts are balanced for static balance and dynamic balance. A crankshaft is statically balanced when the weight of the entire assembly of crankpins, crank cheeks, and flyweights is balanced around the axis of rotation.

notes.front: How does a top overhaul differ from a major overhaul?
notes.back: A top overhaul reconditions the cylinders without complete dismantling; a major overhaul completely reconditions the engine, crankcase disassembled.
notes.explanation: Many hold that an engine needing a top overhaul’s dismantling should get a major overhaul instead.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Top Overhaul”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Many stress that if an engine requires this much dismantling, it should be completely disassembled and receive a major overhaul.

notes.front: How does valve clearance differ between solid and hydraulic lifters?
notes.back: Solid lifters need clearance adjusted by hand with screw and lock nut; hydraulic lifters keep it at zero automatically.
notes.explanation: Clearance checks were a continuous maintenance item until hydraulic lifters were used.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Solid Lifters/Tappets”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: This adjustment or inspection was a continuous maintenance item until hydraulic lifters were used. Hydraulic Valve Tappets/Lifters Some aircraft engines incorporate hydraulic tappets that automatically keep the valve clearance at zero

notes.front: How do compression rings and oil control rings differ in job and position?
notes.back: Compression rings, just below the head, stop gas escaping; oil control rings, below them and above the pin, regulate the oil film.
notes.explanation: Most aircraft engines use two compression rings plus one or more oil control rings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Compression Ring”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: Oil control rings are placed in the grooves immediately below the compression rings and above the piston pin bores.
